notes.title: Units, formulas, resistor code
notes.html:
V = I·RP = V·I = I²·R = V²/RE = P·t (J = W·s; 1 kWh = 3.6×10⁶ J; 1 Wh = 3600 J)Q = I·t (coulombs = amps × seconds)Battery energy: Wh = V × Ah Run time = Wh ÷ WWire: R = ρ·L/A (ρ in Ω·m, A in m²; 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²)Coulomb: F = k·q₁q₂/r², k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ CField: E = F/q (N/C)
QuantityUnitSymbolNamed for
ChargecoulombCCoulomb
CurrentampereAAmpère
VoltagevoltVVolta
ResistanceohmΩOhm
PowerwattWWatt
EnergyjouleJJoule
FrequencyhertzHzHertz

Prefixes: n = 10⁻⁹, µ = 10⁻⁶, m = 10⁻³, k = 10³, M = 10⁶. Convert before you calculate: 15 mA = 0.015 A, 2.2 kΩ = 2200 Ω. Volts ÷ kΩ gives mA.

Significant figures: metric units; give as many significant figures as the least precise number you were given. 12.0 V ÷ 4.0 Ω = 3.0 A.

Resistor color code

0123456789
blackbrownredorangeyellowgreenbluevioletgraywhite

Bands: digit, digit, multiplier (number of zeros), tolerance. Gold ±5%, silver ±10%, brown ±1%. Examples: orange-orange-brown-gold = 330 Ω ±5%; yellow-violet-red-gold = 4.7 kΩ ±5%. Gold and silver as a multiplier (third band) mean ×0.1 and ×0.01. The tolerance band is set apart from the others; read from the end opposite it.

Trap Squaring: P = I²R needs I squared first. Doubling V quadruples P. Doubling a charge doubles F, but doubling the distance cuts F to a quarter.

notes.title: Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)
notes.html:
• Two kinds of charge. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract. Electrons are the mobile charges in solids. Charge is conserved and quantized: one electron is −1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.
  • Field lines point away from + and toward −, in the direction of force on a positive test charge. Field strength E = F/q.
  • Coulomb's Law: F = k·q₁q₂/r². Use meters and coulombs (1 µC = 10⁻⁶ C, 1 nC = 10⁻⁹ C, 1 cm = 0.01 m). The sign only tells you attract or repel.
Worked example. +3.0 µC and +5.0 µC, 0.30 m apart: F = (8.99×10⁹)(3.0×10⁻⁶)(5.0×10⁻⁶)/(0.30)² = 0.1349/0.090 = 1.50 N, repulsive.
Scaling: force ∝ q₁q₂ and ∝ 1/r². Triple r → 1/9. Double one charge and double r → 2/4 = ½.

Charging and polarization

  • Friction (triboelectric): electrons move from one insulator to the other. Glass rubbed with silk: glass loses electrons and becomes positive.
  • Conduction: touching a charged object shares charge, giving the same sign.
  • Induction: a charged rod near (not touching) a neutral conductor moves charge; grounding the far side and removing the ground before the rod leaves a net charge of the opposite sign.
  • Polarization: a neutral insulator (paper, wall) shifts its charges slightly. The nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes, so a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.

Static hazards and control

  • Static has voltage but no continuous current. Sparks can ignite fuel vapor or dust. Electrostatic discharge (ESD) can destroy chips.
  • Dry air builds charge; humid air bleeds it away. Grounding, wrist straps, antistatic mats and bags drain charge safely.

notes.title: DC and AC (area iii)
notes.html:
DCAC
DirectionOne wayReverses periodically
SourcesBatteries, solar cells, fuel cells, rectified supplies, USB chargersAlternators and generators, wall outlets
UsesElectronics, LEDs, motors on batteriesPower distribution (transformers easily change voltage)
Typical1.5, 3, 9, 12 V cells120 V / 60 Hz (US), 230 V / 50 Hz (many countries)
  • Period T = 1/f. 60 Hz → 16.7 ms; 50 Hz → 20 ms.
  • Why AC transmission uses very high voltage: P = VI, so the same power at higher V needs less current, and line loss is I²R.
  • Conventional current flows from + to − outside the source. Electrons move the other way. Slides use conventional current.
  • Cells: in series the voltages add (4 × 1.5 V = 6 V). In parallel the voltage stays the same and capacity adds. Dry cell = paste electrolyte (alkaline, zinc-carbon); wet cell = liquid electrolyte (lead-acid). A battery is two different metals plus an electrolyte, so a lemon or potato works (about 0.7 V per lemon with copper and steel, about 1.2 V per Cu-Zn potato cell).
  • Hazards: current through the body does the damage. About 1 mA is felt, 10 to 20 mA can lock muscles, about 100 mA across the chest can cause fibrillation. Voltage drives that current through body resistance; wet skin means lower resistance. A short circuit (near-0 Ω path) gives huge current, heat, fire. Never demonstrate one.
  • Rectifier: diodes turn AC into DC (a single diode = half-wave).

Household AC (2026 list)

  • US outlet: hot (black, ≈120 V RMS to ground), neutral (white, return path, ≈0 V), ground (green or bare, fault path only).
  • RMS is the DC-equivalent heating value: Vrms = Vpeak/√2, so 120 V RMS ≈ 170 V peak.
  • Breaker panel: 15 A and 20 A branch circuits; GFCI at wet locations. Power in a line is P = VI, so I = P/V.

notes.title: Current, voltage, resistance, power, energy (area iv)
notes.html:
• Voltage is the push (J/C), current is the flow (C/s), resistance is the opposition. Water analogy: pressure = voltage, flow = current, narrow pipe = resistance, pump = battery.
  • Resistance of a wire: R = ρL/A. Longer → more R. Thicker → less R (area goes with diameter squared: double the diameter, R ÷ 4). Hotter metal → more R. ρ: silver 1.59, copper 1.68, gold 2.44, aluminum 2.65 (×10⁻⁸ Ω·m). Glass and rubber ≈ 10¹⁰ to 10¹⁶ Ω·m or more.
  • Ohmic parts have a straight-line I–V graph (slope 1/R). Diodes and LEDs do not.
  • Resistor power rating: a ¼ W, 100 Ω resistor can carry at most √(0.25/100) = 50 mA.
  • Energy: E = P·t. Use kW × hours for kWh and cost; use W × seconds for joules. 60 W × 8 h = 0.48 kWh.
  • Efficiency = output ÷ input.
Battery run time. 3.7 V, 2500 mAh → 3.7 × 2.5 = 9.25 Wh. Into a 2.5 W device → 3.7 h. Into a 100 Ω resistor from 9 V with a 500 mAh cell: I = 0.09 A, t = 0.5/0.09 = 5.6 h.
Trap Mixing units. mAh is not Ah. Minutes are not seconds. Check every number has its base unit before multiplying.

notes.title: DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)
notes.html:
Series: same current; voltages add; R = R₁ + R₂ + …
Parallel: same voltage; currents add; 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …; two: R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂); n equal: R/n. The result is below the smallest branch.
Voltage divider: V₂ = V·R₂/(R₁+R₂). Current divider (two branches): I₁ = I·R₂/(R₁+R₂); the smaller R takes more current.

Method for any network

  1. Reduce parallel groups and series groups one step at a time until one resistor remains.
  2. I_total = V/R_total.
  3. Expand back: find the voltage across each group, then the current in each resistor (V = IR).
  4. Check: branch currents sum to the node current; drops around the loop sum to the source; Σ resistor power = source power.
Worked example. 18 V, R₁ = 6 Ω in series with R₂ = 12 Ω ∥ R₃ = 12 Ω. Parallel pair = 6 Ω; R_total = 12 Ω; I = 1.5 A. Pair voltage = 1.5 × 6 = 9 V; I₂ = I₃ = 0.75 A. Power: 13.5 W + 6.75 W + 6.75 W = 27 W = 18 × 1.5.

Brightness and power

  • Series bulbs: same current, so larger R gets more power (P = I²R).
  • Parallel bulbs: same voltage, so smaller R gets more power (P = V²/R).
  • Remove one parallel bulb: the others do not change. Remove one series bulb: all go out.
  • Add a resistor in series: total R rises, current falls. Add one in parallel: total R falls, current rises.
  • Load on a divider: a load across R₂ makes R₂ ∥ R_load, so the output drops.
  • Maximum power transfer (bonus): load power peaks when R_load = R_source; then half the power is lost in the source.

Open and short circuits

  • Open: break in the path, I = 0. The break shows the full source voltage across it; every other series part shows 0 V.
  • Short: near-zero resistance path. Current is huge; parts in parallel with the short get ~0 V.
  • A switch that is open has the full battery voltage across its terminals.

Meters

  • Voltmeter: in parallel, very high resistance. Ammeter: in series, very low resistance, never across a source. Resistance: power off, isolate the part.
  • Dial: V with a straight line = DC volts; wavy line = AC (never used here). Leads: red in V/Ω, black in COM. Start on the highest range. Current mode acts like a wire; avoid it, or measure V and R and calculate I.
  • Open circuit on an ohmmeter shows OL or blinking digits.

Schematic symbols to know

Resistor (zigzag or rectangle), battery (long line +, short line −), ground (common 0 V), switch, lamp (circle with X), fuse, LED (diode triangle with two arrows), diode (triangle toward cathode), voltmeter (V in a circle), ammeter (A in a circle). Wires that cross with a dot are connected; without a dot they are not.

Trap Parallel formula: 1/R_total is not R_total. Always finish by checking that the answer is smaller than the smallest branch.

notes.title: Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)
notes.html:
• KCL: current into a node = current out. (Charge is conserved.)
  • KVL: the sum of voltage rises and drops around any closed loop = 0. (Energy is conserved.)

Two-loop recipe (two unknowns at most)

  1. Label a current in each branch and pick directions. A wrong guess just gives a negative answer.
  2. Write KCL at one node.
  3. Write KVL around two independent loops. A resistor is a drop in the direction of current; a source is a rise when you go through it from − to +.
  4. Solve the pair of equations. Check that power supplied = power dissipated.
Example. E₁ = 19 V and R₁ = 2 Ω on the left, E₂ = 17 V and R₂ = 4 Ω on the right, R₃ = 6 Ω shared. I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 19 = 2I₁ + 6I₃; 17 = 4I₂ + 6I₃. Substitute: 19 = 8I₁ + 6I₂ and 17 = 6I₁ + 10I₂, so I₁ = 2.0 A, I₂ = 0.5 A, I₃ = 2.5 A.

notes.title: Control devices (area vi)
notes.html:
DeviceWhat it does
SPST switchOne pole, one throw: simple on/off
SPDT switchCommon terminal connects to one of two others
DPDT switchTwo poles switched together; cross-wire it to reverse a motor
RelaySmall coil current closes contacts in a separate circuit (NO = open at rest, NC = closed at rest). Add a reverse diode across the coil.
FuseMetal element melts on overcurrent; replace it. In series with the load. Slow-blow tolerates brief surges (motors).
Circuit breakerTrips on overcurrent (heat bends a bimetal strip; a coil handles big shorts); resettable
GFCITrips when hot and neutral currents differ by about 5 mA (leak to ground, e.g. through a person). Protects people.
  • Fuse size: I = P/V, then choose the smallest standard rating at or above I. 90 W at 12 V = 7.5 A → 10 A.
  • Breaker check: I = P/V. A 2400 W load on 120 V draws 20 A and trips a 15 A breaker.
  • Switch logic: switches in series = AND (both closed to light). Switches in parallel = OR (either closed).
  • Three-way circuit: two SPDT switches. The commons go to the source (switch 1) and the lamp (switch 2); two traveler wires join the other terminals. Flipping either switch toggles the lamp.

notes.title: Diodes and LEDs (area vii)
notes.html:
• Silicon PN junction: P-type (holes) joined to N-type (electrons) forms a depletion region with a barrier of about 0.7 V. Forward bias (anode positive) narrows it; reverse bias widens it.
  • Forward-biased silicon diode conducts with about 0.7 V drop. Reverse biased: acts like an open switch (tiny leakage) until breakdown.
  • LED: a diode that emits light. Forward drop about 1.8 to 2.2 V red/yellow/green, about 3 V blue/white. Longer lead = anode; flat side = cathode.
  • LED resistor: R = (V_supply − V_f)/I. Round up to a standard value, never down. P = I²R (check the ¼ W rating).
  • Series LEDs: same current; drops add; the supply must exceed the sum. Parallel LEDs: give each its own resistor.
  • Diode drops add in series: two silicon diodes = 1.4 V.
  • Uses: rectifier (AC to DC), reverse-polarity protection (series diode, costs 0.7 V), flyback protection across relay coils, Zener (reverse breakdown for a fixed voltage), photodiode and solar cell (light makes current).
Worked example. 9.0 V, LED 2.1 V, 15 mA max. R = 6.9/0.015 = 460 Ω → use 470 Ω (I = 14.7 mA). A 390 Ω resistor would give 17.7 mA.

notes.title: Digital logic and binary (area viii)
notes.html:
A BANDORNANDNORXORXNOR
0 0001101
0 1011010
1 0011010
1 1110001
  • Precedence: NOT, then AND, then OR. n inputs = 2ⁿ truth-table rows.
  • Gate tricks: AND with 1 passes the input, AND with 0 gives 0. OR with 0 passes, OR with 1 gives 1. XOR with 1 inverts, XOR with 0 passes.
  • De Morgan: (AB)′ = A′ + B′ and (A + B)′ = A′B′. Break the bar, flip the operator. So A′B′ = NOR, and NAND of inverted inputs = OR.
  • Identities: A + AB = A, A(A + B) = A, AB + AB′ = A, A + A′B = A + B, A(A′ + B) = AB, AB + AB′ + A′B = A + B.
  • Universal gates: NAND and NOR. With NAND: NOT = 1 gate (tie inputs), AND = 2, OR = 3, NOR = 4, XOR = 4. With NOR: NOT = 1, OR = 2.
  • Truth table to expression: write an AND term for each 1 row (complement the variables that are 0), then OR the terms, then simplify.
  • Multiplexer: n select lines choose among 2ⁿ inputs. 2:1: Y = S′A + SB. A mux with a data input tied to 0 or B can act as AND (select = A, I₀ = 0, I₁ = B).
  • Half adder: Sum = A ⊕ B, Carry = A·B. Full adder: Sum = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Carry = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B). The sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1. A ripple adder chains full adders.

Binary

  • Place values: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. 101101 = 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.
  • Decimal to binary: subtract the largest power of 2, repeat. 37 = 32 + 4 + 1 = 100101.
  • Addition: 0+0 = 0, 0+1 = 1, 1+1 = 10 (carry 1), 1+1+1 = 11. Adding two n-bit numbers needs up to n + 1 bits. n bits hold 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.
  • Check by converting to decimal: 1101 + 1001 = 13 + 9 = 22 = 10110.

notes.title: Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)
notes.html:
Connectives: ∧ and, ∨ or, → if…then, ~ not, ↔ if and only if. The antecedent is the "if" part. Find the main connective by commas and "both…and", "either…or", "if…then".

RuleForm
Modus ponensP→Q, P ∴ Q
Modus tollensP→Q, ~Q ∴ ~P
Hypothetical syllogismP→Q, Q→R ∴ P→R
Disjunctive syllogismP∨Q, ~P ∴ Q
Conjunctive elimination / additionP∧Q ∴ P; P, Q ∴ P∧Q
Disjunctive additionP ∴ P∨Q
Constructive dilemmaP→Q, R→S, P∨R ∴ Q∨S
Double negation, tautology, commutation~~P = P; P∨P = P; P∨Q = Q∨P
EquivalenceP↔Q = (P→Q)∧(Q→P)
De Morgan~(P∧Q) = ~P∨~Q; ~(P∨Q) = ~P∧~Q
Trap Affirming the consequent (Q, so P) and denying the antecedent (~P, so ~Q) are invalid. In a proof, P in the reason column means premise.

notes.title: Magnetism and induction (adjacent)
notes.html:
Listed on the 2026 Division B page; absent from the 2027 text you were given. Learn the basics in case they return.

  • Poles: like repel, unlike attract. Field lines leave N, enter S, never cross; closer lines = stronger field. Earth’s geographic north is a magnetic south pole. Iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted; copper, aluminum and gold are not.
  • Ørsted: current makes a magnetic field. Straight wire (right-hand rule): thumb along conventional current, fingers curl the way the field circles. Coil: fingers curl with the current, thumb points to the N pole.
  • Electromagnet strength: more turns, more current, soft iron core. It switches off with the current.
  • Motor: electrical → mechanical (force on a current in a field, F = BIL; the commutator reverses current each half turn). Generator: mechanical → electrical.
  • Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage. Faster motion, stronger magnet and more turns give more voltage. Lenz: the induced current opposes the change.
  • Transformer (AC only): Vs/Vp = Ns/Np. Ideal: Pin = Pout, so stepping voltage down steps current up by the same ratio.
  • Units: tesla (T) for flux density, N/(A·m).
Electromagnet station. Wrap many turns of insulated wire around an iron bolt, connect a battery, test with paper clips. More turns or a second cell picks up more. Keep it brief: the wire and battery heat up.

notes.title: Capacitance (adjacent)
notes.html:
• Two conductors separated by an insulator. C = Q/V (farad; usually µF). Energy E = ½CV² (doubling V gives 4× the energy).
  • Parallel plates: C grows with plate area and with a dielectric, shrinks as the gap grows.
  • Parallel: C adds. Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (opposite of resistors).
  • Once charged in DC, it acts like an open circuit. Electrolytic capacitors are polarized: wrong polarity can fail.
Example. 100 µF at 12 V: Q = 1.2 mC; E = 7.2 mJ.

written: Explain the difference between a fuse and a circuit breaker when current gets too high. Which one protects people from shock?

A fuse has a thin metal element that melts when the current is too high; it opens once and must be replaced. A circuit breaker trips (heat bends a bimetal strip or a coil reacts to a surge) and can be reset. Neither is the shock device: a GFCI protects people by tripping when hot and neutral currents differ by about 5 mA.
Explain why a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.

The balloon’s charge polarizes the wall: opposite charge shifts toward the surface nearest the balloon and like charge shifts away. Coulomb force falls with distance squared, so the nearer opposite charge attracts more strongly than the farther like charge repels, and the net force is attraction.
Describe how to find an unknown resistor Rx using only a voltmeter, a battery and a known resistor.

Connect the known resistor R in series with Rx across the battery. Measure V across R and across Rx. The series current is I = V_R / R. Then Rx = V_x / I = R × V_x / V_R. Power off before rewiring, keep the meter in parallel, and optionally check Rx with the ohm setting with the part isolated.
Design the wiring that makes two identical LEDs equally bright from one 9 V battery. State your resistor value if the LEDs drop 2.0 V and run at 15 mA.

Give each LED its own series resistor of equal value, and connect the two branches in parallel across the battery. R = (9.0 − 2.0)/0.015 = 467 Ω, so use 470 Ω (14.9 mA). Each resistor dissipates I²R ≈ 0.10 W, within a ¼ W rating. Check LED polarity: long lead (anode) toward the resistor and battery positive.
Why does long-distance power transmission use very high AC voltage?

For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current. Heat loss in the line is I²R, so lower current greatly cuts the loss. AC can be stepped up and down with transformers, so it is used for distribution, then stepped down for homes.
Show how to build a NOT gate, an AND gate and an OR gate from NAND gates only, and give the gate counts.

NOT: tie both NAND inputs together (1 gate). AND: NAND followed by a NOT-connected NAND (2 gates). OR: invert each input with a NAND, then NAND the two results (3 gates), because A + B = (A′·B′)′ by De Morgan.
A series loop of a battery, a switch and a lamp is dead. The battery reads 9 V at its terminals. The lamp reads 0 V. The switch reads 9 V. Name the fault and explain how you know.

The switch is open (or has a faulty contact). With no current, the lamp has no drop. Kirchhoff’s voltage law puts the whole source voltage across the one element with the break, which is the switch. Power off, then check the switch contacts and its wires.
A 24 V source feeds R1 = 8 Ω in series with R2 = 24 Ω in parallel with R3 = 12 Ω. Find R_total, the source current, the current in R3 and the power in R1. Show your work.
bench: Mystery resistor (voltage only)
Put a known R in series with Rx across the supply. Measure V across each. R<sub>x</sub> = R<sub>known</sub> × V<sub>x</sub>/V<sub>known</sub>. Report with correct significant figures and units.
Power supplied to a circuit
Voltmeter across the circuit (parallel), ammeter in series. P = V·I. If told to avoid current mode, calculate I from a known resistor’s voltage.
Two equally bright LEDs
Same LED type, each with its own series resistor of the same value, branches in parallel on one battery. Resistor from R = (V − Vf)/I. Check polarity.
USB charger and battery
Read the label for each output level (V and A). P = V·I for each. Battery Wh = V × Ah. Time = Wh ÷ W (divide by efficiency if given).
Logic from a truth table
Write the Boolean expression from the rows with output 1, simplify, then choose gates. For Y = A·B′ use a NOT on B into an AND. Verify every row.
Troubleshoot a faulty circuit

Power off. Look for loose, reversed or missing parts. Power on and measure across each element. The element showing the full source voltage in a series loop is open. A part with 0 V and others too high suggests a short.
Wire a three-way switch
Switch 1 common to the source, switch 2 common to the lamp, travelers join the other terminals, lamp returns to the battery. Test all four switch positions.
Create a target resistance
Choose series (add) and parallel (R₁R₂/(R₁+R₂)) combinations from the parts. Verify with the meter before applying power.
Breadboard and meter basics

Short 5-hole columns are connected on each side of the center gap. Long edge rails run the full length (check for a split in the middle). Red lead V/Ω, black COM, DC volts with the straight line symbol.
Electromagnet (2026 list)
Wind insulated wire around an iron bolt (20+ turns), connect one battery, count paper clips lifted. Double the turns, compare. Disconnect between trials.

questions.q: For which inputs (A,B) does a 2-input XOR gate output 1?

sol: XOR output is 1 when the inputs DIFFER. So it is 1 for: (0,1) and (1,0).

questions.q: For which inputs (A,B) does a 2-input NOR gate output 1?

questions.q: In 1820 Ørsted saw a compass needle swing when it was placed near a wire carrying current. What did this show?
o: A current produces a magnetic effect
Static charge on the wire pulls on iron
The wire was heating the air around the needle
Gravity from the wire bends the needle
questions.w: Ørsted's compass result was the first link between electricity and magnetism.
sol: A compass needle is a tiny magnet, so it only reacts to magnetic effects.
The needle moved only while current flowed, so the current made the magnetic effect.
Heat and static charge do not turn a compass; this was a new discovery.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which scientist discovered in 1820 that a current deflects a compass needle? (Spell it any way you like.)
questions.w: Hans Christian Ørsted (also spelled Oersted) found the first electricity and magnetism link.
sol: Compass needle = tiny magnet.
Only a magnetic effect from the wire can turn it.
Ørsted, 1820. Ampère followed within weeks.
From your notes · History (area i): Ørsted1820Current deflects a compass: first link of electricity and magnetism
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: What could the voltaic pile of 1800 do that rubbing amber or glass could not?
questions.w: Volta's pile was the first source of steady current instead of one-shot static sparks.
sol: Friction machines gave short sparks.
A pile uses chemical reactions between metals and a wet cloth, which keep going.
A steady current is what circuits need.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Who is credited with naming the two kinds of charge positive and negative?
questions.w: Benjamin Franklin introduced + and − and the idea of conventional current.
sol: Franklin studied charge in the 1700s.
He labeled the charges + and −.
His guess about flow direction is why conventional current runs + to −.
From your notes · History (area i): The slides also name Thales (amber), Franklin (naming + and −, conventional current), Tesla (AC).
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: In Boole's algebra, what is 1 AND 0?
questions.w: AND gives 1 only when every input is 1.
sol: AND means both must be true.
Here one input is 0.
So the answer is 0.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: In Boole's algebra, what is 1 OR 0?
questions.w: OR gives 1 when at least one input is 1.
sol: OR means either one is enough.
One input is 1.
So the answer is 1.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which unit is named for the Scottish engineer James Watt?
o: The watt, a unit of power
The volt, a unit of potential difference
The joule, a unit of charge
The farad, a unit of energy
questions.w: The watt measures power: energy per second.
sol: Watt, volt and farad are all people's names.
The watt is the rate of using energy.
One watt = one joule per second.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: US wall outlets supply alternating current. How many cycles per second (in Hz) does it go through?
questions.w: In the US, mains AC is 60 Hz (50 Hz in much of the world).
sol: AC reverses direction again and again.
Hertz means cycles per second.
US power is 60 Hz.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Put these in order, earliest first.
sol: Coulomb is the earliest, from the 1780s.
Volta made the battery in 1800.
Faraday found induction in 1831, and Hertz made radio waves in 1887.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which scientist is matched with the quantity their unit measures?
questions.w: The farad is the unit of capacitance.
sol: Faraday = farad = capacitance.
Hertz = frequency, Ohm = resistance, Volta = voltage.
Current is the ampere.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: The ancient Greek word for amber, which Thales noticed attracts light objects after rubbing, gave us which modern word?
questions.w: Greek elektron means amber; rubbed amber showed static electricity.
sol: Amber was one of the first known things to show static charge.
The Greek word elektron became 'electric'.
Magnetism comes from lodestones, a different story.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Match each unit to what it equals.
questions.w: Each unit is a ratio of other quantities.
sol: Current is charge per time.
Voltage is energy per charge; resistance is voltage per current.
Power is energy per time; capacitance is charge per volt.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Ørsted showed that a current makes a magnetic effect. Faraday's discovery is the reverse. What is it?
o: A changing magnetic field can create a voltage and current
A current cannot flow in a magnet
Static charge can make a magnet
questions.w: Ørsted: electricity to magnetism. Faraday: magnetism to electricity.
sol: Faraday moved magnets near coils in 1831.
A changing magnetic field pushes charges, giving a voltage (induction).
This is how generators work.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Ørsted: current makes a magnetic field.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A power-plant generator turns a magnet inside coils of wire. Whose discovery does it use?
questions.w: Moving magnets near coils induces a voltage: induction.
sol: Generators need a changing magnetic field through a coil.
That is Faraday's induction.
Volta's pile is a chemical battery and has no motion.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: AC power at 60 Hz goes through how many complete cycles in 3.0 s?
questions.w: 1 Hz = 1 cycle per second.
sol: Cycles = frequency × time.
A common slip is to give 60, one second's worth.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: What is the period of 50 Hz AC, in milliseconds?
questions.w: Period = 1 / frequency.
sol: Period T = 1/f.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: What is the period of 60 Hz AC, in milliseconds? Round to 0.1.
questions.w: Period = 1 / frequency.
sol: That is 0.01667 s.
Convert to ms: 16.7 ms.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: In 1937 Claude Shannon showed that Boole's algebra could describe what?
o: Networks of relay and switch circuits
questions.w: Boole's 0 and 1 map onto open and closed switches.
sol: Switch on or off is two-valued, like Boole's 0 and 1.
Shannon used Boolean algebra to design switching circuits.
This is the basis of digital logic.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Kirchhoff's current law: 5.0 A flows into a junction. 2.0 A leaves in one wire and 1.5 A in another. What current leaves in the third wire?
questions.w: Charge in equals charge out at a node.
sol: Charge cannot pile up at a node.
Out total must be 5.0 A.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Why did power companies choose AC for long-distance power lines?
o: Transformers can step the voltage up, which lowers the current and the heat loss in the wires
AC electrons move faster than DC electrons
questions.w: High voltage means low current, and low current wastes little power as heat.
sol: Wire loss is I²R, so lower current wastes much less.
Transformers work only with changing (AC) current.
AC wires still have resistance, and DC lights bulbs fine.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): Why AC transmission uses very high voltage: P = VI, so the same power at higher V needs less current, and line loss is I²R.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Match each scientist to the unit named for them.
questions.w: Many SI electrical units honor these scientists.
sol: Volt = potential difference.
Hertz = frequency; farad = capacitance.
Coulomb = charge; ohm = resistance.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Name the American scientist whose name is on the unit of inductance (the henry).
questions.w: Joseph Henry discovered induction independently of Faraday.
sol: Inductance is measured in henrys.
The unit honors Joseph Henry.
He found self-induction too.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Galvani saw frog legs twitch near two different metals. Volta argued the electricity came from:
o: the contact of the two different metals
questions.w: Volta's view led to the pile: two metals plus an electrolyte.
sol: Galvani thought the frog made the electricity.
Volta tested stacks of metal and found current without any animal.
That led to the first battery.

From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): A battery is two different metals plus an electrolyte, so a lemon or potato works (about 0.7 V per lemon with copper and steel, about 1.2 V per Cu-Zn potato cell).
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Franklin guessed that current flows from + to −. We now know that in a metal wire the moving charges are electrons. Why do we still use Franklin's 'conventional current'?
o: Circuit rules give the same results either way, and the convention is standard
Electrons really do flow from + to −
Franklin's rule makes the math work only for batteries
questions.w: Conventional current is a bookkeeping choice that still works.
sol: Electrons move from − toward +.
A positive charge moving one way acts like a negative charge moving the other way.
So the rules for V, I and R stay valid.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Straight wire (right-hand rule): thumb along conventional current, fingers curl the way the field circles.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Who discovered the electron in 1897 while studying cathode rays?
questions.w: J. J. Thomson showed cathode rays are tiny negative particles.
sol: Cathode rays bend in electric fields toward +.
So they carry negative charge.
Thomson named them electrons (corpuscles at first).
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: In the 'war of the currents', Edison's early power stations supplied which type of electricity?
questions.w: Edison used DC; Tesla and Westinghouse promoted AC.
sol: DC flows one way only.
Edison's 1880s New York system used DC.
AC won for long lines because transformers could raise voltage.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: The Leyden jar of the 1740s stored charge. Which modern part does it most resemble?
questions.w: Two conductors (foil inside and out) separated by glass hold charge: a capacitor.
sol: It stored charge between two conducting layers.
That is what a capacitor does.
The farad honors Faraday.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Put these events in order, earliest first.
sol: Ørsted and Faraday are in the first half of the 1800s.
Kirchhoff is 1845 and Boole 1854.
Hertz is last, in 1887.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which unit equals one joule per second?
questions.w: Power is energy per time.
sol: A joule is energy.
Per second gives a rate.
One joule per second is one watt.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which scientist's name is on the unit of magnetic flux density?
questions.w: The tesla (T) measures magnetic flux density.
sol: Tesla also developed AC systems.
The unit of flux density is the tesla.
It is named for Nikola Tesla.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Select ALL that are SI units named for scientists.
questions.w: Second is a time unit with no person's name.
sol: Volta, Hertz and Faraday are all honored.
The second is not named after anyone.
So volt, hertz and farad are the correct picks.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Before the voltaic pile (1800), experimenters mostly had which sources of electricity?
questions.w: Only static sources existed until Volta.
sol: They could make sparks by rubbing.
Leyden jars stored that charge briefly.
No steady source existed until the pile.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Coulomb's law of electric force and Newton's law of gravity share which feature?
o: Force falls off with the square of the distance
questions.w: Both are inverse-square laws, but electric force can repel and is far stronger.
sol: Both ∝ 1/r².
Electric force depends on charge, not mass, and can push or pull.
Gravity is only attractive.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A wire with current is held over a compass. How does the needle behave?
o: It turns away from its north-pointing direction
It stays still because current has no magnetic effect
It points straight at the wire
questions.w: Current makes a magnetic field that the compass needle follows.
sol: The needle follows the combined field of Earth and the wire.
That moves it off north.
It does not spin or point at the wire.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A pile has 30 identical cells in series, each giving 0.90 V. What is the total voltage?
questions.w: Series voltages add.
sol: Series cells stack their voltages.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: One ohm is equal to one:
questions.w: Ohm's law R = V/I.
sol: R = V ÷ I.
So ohm = volt ÷ ampere.
Coulomb per second is the ampere; joule per coulomb is the volt.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: One watt is equal to one:
questions.w: Power P = V × I.
sol: Power = voltage × current.
That is volt × ampere.
Volt ÷ ampere is the ohm.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A 10 kW load is fed through a line with 2.0 Ω resistance at 1000 V. How many watts are lost as heat in the line?
questions.w: Current I = P/V, loss = I²R.
sol: Loss = I²R = 10² × 2.0 = 200 W.
Do not use V²/R: 1000 V is the supply voltage, not the voltage across the line.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Sending the same power at 10 times higher voltage cuts the line's heat loss by what factor?
questions.w: Loss = I²R and I = P/V.
sol: 10 times the voltage means 1/10 the current.
Loss ∝ I², so 1/100.
The loss is 100 times smaller.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A plant sends 50 kW through lines with total resistance 0.40 Ω at 500 V. What percent of the power is lost in the lines?
questions.w: I = 100 A, so loss = 4000 W.
sol: Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: The same plant (50 kW, 0.40 Ω line) steps up to 5000 V. How many watts are lost in the lines?
questions.w: I falls to 10 A.
sol: = 40 W, 100 times less than at 500 V.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A transformer is wired to a steady DC battery. After the switch is closed, the output voltage is zero. Why?
o: Induction needs a changing magnetic field, and steady DC gives a constant one
Transformers only work with static charge
The primary coil has no resistance
questions.w: Faraday's induction needs changing flux.
sol: A constant current makes a constant magnetic field.
A coil only gets a voltage when the field through it changes.
AC changes all the time, so transformers use AC.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Induction (Faraday): a changing flux through a coil induces a voltage.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which statement best contrasts Ørsted and Faraday?
o: Ørsted: current makes a magnetic effect. Faraday: a changing magnetic field makes a voltage
Ørsted: magnets make current. Faraday: current makes magnets
Both showed that static charge makes magnets
questions.w: They are opposite directions of the same link.
sol: Ørsted (1820) went from electricity to magnetism.
Faraday (1831) went from magnetism to electricity.
Mixing the two is the common error.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A magnet is held perfectly still inside a coil connected to a meter. What current does the meter show?
o: A steady current proportional to the magnet's strength
A current that grows with time
questions.w: Induction needs change, not just a magnetic field.
sol: Faraday found a current only while the field changes.
A still magnet means no change in flux.
So the reading is zero.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil first slowly, then quickly. Compared with the slow push, the quick push gives:
questions.w: Induced voltage depends on how fast the magnetic flux changes.
sol: Faster motion = faster change.
Induced voltage grows with the rate of change.
Speed matters, not just the magnet's presence.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A magnet pushed into a coil over 0.50 s induces 0.40 V. If the same push takes 0.10 s, how many volts are induced?
questions.w: Induced voltage ∝ rate of change of flux (1/time).
sol: Same flux change, 5 times faster.
So 5 times the voltage.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A coil gives 0.40 V. Now the magnet moves twice as fast through a coil with twice as many turns. How many volts?
questions.w: Voltage ∝ turns × speed.
sol: Twice the speed doubles the voltage.
Twice the turns doubles it again.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Hertz's radio-wave experiments of the 1880s confirmed whose prediction?
questions.w: Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves; Hertz made and detected them.
sol: Maxwell's equations predicted waves moving at light speed.
Hertz generated them with sparks and detected them across a room.
He also showed they reflect and refract like light.
From your notes · History (area i): Hertz1887Generated and detected electromagnetic (radio) waves; the hertz = 1 cycle per second
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Hertz showed radio waves reflect, bend and polarize like light. What did this suggest about light?
o: Light is also an electromagnetic wave
Light is a flow of electrons in a wire
Light is a magnetic field only
questions.w: Same behavior pointed to the same kind of wave.
sol: Radio waves are electromagnetic.
They act like light in many tests.
So light is an electromagnetic wave of higher frequency.
From your notes · History (area i): Hertz1887Generated and detected electromagnetic (radio) waves; the hertz = 1 cycle per second
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A radio station transmits at 100 MHz. What is the wavelength in meters? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
questions.w: Wavelength = c / f.
sol: λ = c/f.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A transmitter makes waves 0.60 m long. What is their frequency in MHz? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
questions.w: f = c / λ.
sol: f = c/λ.
That is 500 MHz.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Evaluate in Boole's algebra: (1 AND 0) OR (NOT 0). Give 0 or 1.
questions.w: Work the brackets first.
sol: NOT 0 = 1.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Evaluate NOT(A AND B) OR C for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0. Give 0 or 1.
questions.w: Work inside out.
sol: A AND B = 1.
NOT 1 = 0.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: De Morgan (a contemporary of Boole) showed that NOT(A AND B) equals:
questions.w: Test with A = 1, B = 0: NOT(0) = 1 and (0 OR 1) = 1.
sol: Try A=1, B=0: A AND B = 0, so NOT gives 1.
(NOT A) OR (NOT B) = 0 OR 1 = 1 (matches).
(NOT A) AND (NOT B) = 0 AND 1 = 0 (does not).
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: How many different input combinations does a 4-input Boolean circuit have?
questions.w: Each input has 2 values.
sol: Each input is 0 or 1.
Combinations = 2⁴.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: The I–V graph of a light-bulb filament curves, because its resistance rises as it heats up. What does that say about Ohm's law V = IR?
o: R = V/I still defines resistance at each point, but R is not constant
Ohm's law is false for all conductors
The bulb has zero resistance when cold
The current is independent of voltage
questions.w: Ohm's 'law' means constant R; V/I is still defined everywhere.
sol: A straight I–V line means constant R (ohmic).
A curve means R changes with V (temperature).
V = IR still works as a definition at each point.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Ohm found that doubling the voltage across a metal wire at steady temperature does what to the current?
questions.w: I = V/R with R constant.
sol: Current ∝ voltage for an ohmic wire.
Double V, double I.
Quadrupling would need V².
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Coulomb's torsion balance twists 8.0° when two charged spheres are 0.10 m apart. Twist is proportional to force. How many degrees will it twist at 0.05 m, with the same charges?
questions.w: Halving r multiplies force by 4.
sol: Force ∝ 1/r².
Half the distance gives 4 times the force.
From your notes · History (area i): Coulomb1785Inverse-square force between charges (torsion balance); unit of charge
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Why was a stack of metal discs separated by wet (brine-soaked) cloth able to make current?
o: The brine lets ions move between the two metals so each cell completes its circuit
The cloth insulates so no charge moves
The brine supplies electrons by itself
questions.w: Two metals plus an electrolyte make a chemical cell.
sol: A cell needs two unlike metals and an electrolyte.
Ions carry charge through the brine.
Stacking cells in series adds voltage.

From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): A battery is two different metals plus an electrolyte, so a lemon or potato works (about 0.7 V per lemon with copper and steel, about 1.2 V per Cu-Zn potato cell).
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Two parallel wires carry current in the same direction and attract. If the current in one wire is reversed, the force becomes:
questions.w: Ampère: same-direction currents attract, opposite-direction currents repel.
sol: Same direction attracts (Ampère, 1820s).
Reversing one current flips the force.
So the wires repel.
From your notes · History (area i): Ampère1820sFounded electrodynamics; parallel currents attract or repel; link between electricity and magnetism; the ampere
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A 9.0 V cell and a 3.0 V cell are in series but facing each other (opposing) across a 12 Ω resistor. How much current flows, in amperes?
questions.w: Net voltage is the difference.
sol: Opposing sources subtract: 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 V.
Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Kirchhoff's current law: 3.2 A and 1.1 A flow into a junction and 2.0 A flows out one wire. What current flows out of the other wire?
questions.w: In = out.
sol: Total in = 4.3 A.
One wire carries away 2.0 A.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Millikan's oil-drop experiment (1909) found that the charge on each drop was:
o: a whole-number multiple of one smallest charge
questions.w: Charge is quantized in units of e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.
sol: Drops had charges like e, 2e, 3e.
No fractions of e were seen.
That showed charge comes in lumps.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which expression equals one watt?
questions.w: P = I²R.
sol: P = VI and V = IR, so P = I²R.
Volt ÷ ohm is the ampere.
Ampere ÷ volt is the siemens.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which named unit equals one ampere × one ohm?
questions.w: V = IR.
sol: Ohm's law: V = I × R.
So amp × ohm = volt.
Watt would be amp × volt.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Match each discovery to the year (best-known date).
questions.w: A timeline helps tie names to ideas.
sol: Volta 1800.
Ørsted 1820, Faraday 1831.
Kirchhoff 1845, Hertz late 1880s.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Siemens (S) is the SI unit of conductance, honoring Werner von Siemens. How is it related to the ohm?
questions.w: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance.
sol: Resistance R = V/I.
Conductance G = I/V = 1/R.
So siemens = ohm⁻¹.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Millikan, Thomson and Coulomb all helped explain charge. Which is matched correctly?
questions.w: Thomson found the electron (1897); Millikan measured its charge (1909).
sol: Thomson = electron discovery.
Millikan = size of its charge.
Coulomb = force between charges.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Tesla's AC induction motor spins without electrical contact to its rotor. What lets the rotor turn?
o: A rotating magnetic field induces current in the rotor
questions.w: Faraday induction plus a rotating field (from polyphase AC).
sol: Polyphase AC makes a rotating magnetic field.
That field induces currents in the rotor.
The induced currents feel a force, so the rotor turns.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Motor: electrical → mechanical (force on a current in a field, F = BIL; the commutator reverses current each half turn).
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A student says: 'Ohm's law shows current is used up as it passes through resistors.' Which Kirchhoff idea corrects this?
o: Charge is conserved, so the current is the same coming out of a series resistor as going in
Voltage is used up so current is too
questions.w: Current is flow of charge, which cannot vanish.
sol: KCL: current in = current out.
Energy, not current, is used up (the voltage drops).
This is the voltage-law and current-law contrast.
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: Which pair correctly links the history to the physical law each person found?
o: Kirchhoff: charge and energy are conserved in circuits
Ohm: charge is conserved at nodes
Volta: energy is conserved around loops
questions.w: KCL = charge conservation; KVL = energy conservation.
sol: Kirchhoff covers both laws.
Ohm relates V, I, R.
Hertz did waves; Coulomb did the force law.
From your notes · History (area i): Kirchhoff1845Current law (charge conservation) and voltage law (energy conservation)
Notes|n2|History (area i)

questions.q: A balloon rubbed on hair gains electrons. The balloon is now:
questions.w: Gaining electrons makes an object negative.
sol: Electrons carry negative charge.
More electrons than protons means net negative.
Protons stay put.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Which particles move when an object is charged by rubbing?
questions.w: Only electrons are free to move between materials.
sol: Protons are held in nuclei.
Electrons are loosely held at the outside.
Rubbing moves electrons.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Which material holds static charge best?
questions.w: Insulators keep charge in place; conductors let it spread and escape.
sol: Plastic is an insulator.
Metals and salt water conduct.
Charge cannot easily leave an insulator.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A neutral object contains:
o: equal amounts of positive and negative charge
questions.w: Neutral means the charges balance, not that they are absent.
sol: Atoms hold protons and electrons.
Equal numbers means net zero.
Charges can still shift (polarization).
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Electric field arrows around an isolated positive point charge point:
questions.w: Field points the way a positive test charge is pushed.
sol: A positive test charge is repelled by +.
So the arrows point outward.
Toward is for negative sources.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): Field lines point away from + and toward −, in the direction of force on a positive test charge.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Which of these is a good conductor?
questions.w: Metals have free electrons.
sol: Free electrons carry charge.
Copper has many.
Rubber, wood and glass are insulators.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Electric field lines drawn closer together show where the field is:
questions.w: Line density shows field strength.
sol: More lines per area means stronger field.
Spread lines mean weaker.
Direction is given by arrows.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Silk rubbed on glass gives the glass +2 nC of charge. What happens to the silk?
questions.w: Charge is conserved: the total stays zero.
sol: Electrons moved from glass to silk.
Silk gained what glass lost.
So the silk is −2 nC.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Proton and electron charges compared: they are
o: equal in size and opposite in sign
equal in size and the same sign
questions.w: Both have magnitude 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C.
sol: A proton is +e.
An electron is −e.
That is why atoms are neutral.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Two charges, +2.0 µC and +3.0 µC, are 0.60 m apart. Find the force between them in newtons. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: F = kq₁q₂/r².
sol: Convert µC to C.
≈ 0.15 N, repulsive.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A rod gains 5.0×10¹² extra electrons. What is its charge in µC? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C; give the magnitude)
questions.w: Q = ne.
sol: = 0.80 µC (negative).
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A 5.0 nC test charge feels a force of 2.0×10⁻⁴ N. What is the electric field strength, in N/C?
questions.w: E = F/q.
sol: Convert nC to C: 5.0×10⁻⁹ C.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A 4.0 µC charge sits in a field of 2500 N/C. What force acts on it, in newtons?
questions.w: F = qE.
sol: Rearrange E = F/q to F = qE.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A charged metal sphere (+6 µC) touches an identical neutral sphere, then they are separated. Each sphere has:
questions.w: Identical conductors share total charge equally.
sol: Total charge +6 µC is conserved.
Two identical spheres split it evenly.
Each gets +3 µC.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A negatively charged rod is brought near, not touching, the knob of a neutral electroscope. The leaves:
o: spread apart, then collapse when the rod is removed
spread and stay spread after the rod leaves
questions.w: Charge is only shifted, not added.
sol: The rod pushes electrons down to the leaves.
The leaves repel, so they spread.
Remove the rod and the electrons return, so they collapse.

From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): Induction: a charged rod near (not touching) a neutral conductor moves charge; grounding the far side and removing the ground before the rod leaves a net charge of the opposite sign.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A positive rod touches a neutral metal sphere on an insulating stand, then is removed. The sphere is:
questions.w: Conduction gives the same sign as the rod.
sol: Electrons flow from the sphere to the rod.
The sphere loses electrons.
So it ends positive.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: One of two point charges is cut to half its value. The distance stays the same. The force becomes:
questions.w: Force ∝ q₁q₂.
sol: Force is proportional to each charge.
Half a charge gives half the force.
Only distance has the squared effect.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: On a conductor in equilibrium, excess charge sits:
questions.w: Like charges repel and spread out as far as possible.
sol: Free charges repel each other.
They move to the outside surface.
Inside a conductor in equilibrium the field is zero.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: An electron is placed in an electric field that points east. The force on the electron points:
questions.w: Force on a negative charge is opposite to the field.
sol: Field direction = force on a positive test charge.
An electron is negative.
So its force is opposite: west.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Why can electric field lines never cross?
o: The field has one direction at any point
questions.w: At a crossing, the field would have two directions at once.
sol: Each point has a single field direction.
Crossing lines would give two.
So lines never cross.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): Field lines point away from + and toward −, in the direction of force on a positive test charge.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Why are fuel trucks grounded or bonded to the tank when they fuel?
o: To drain static charge so a spark cannot ignite fuel vapor
To make the fuel flow faster
questions.w: Sparks can ignite vapor; grounding drains the charge.
sol: Flow can build static charge.
A spark may ignite vapor.
Grounding lets charge leak away safely.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): Sparks can ignite fuel vapor or dust.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Which charge could exist on an object? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.w: Charge is quantized: a whole number times e.
sol: 2.403×10⁻¹⁹ = 1.5e, not allowed.
Fractions of e do not appear.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A body has a charge of −4.806×10⁻¹⁹ C. How many excess electrons does it have? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.w: N = Q/e.
sol: Charge comes in whole electrons.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A charged object comes near a neutral insulator, shifting its charges slightly without a net charge change. What is this called?
questions.w: The nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes.
sol: Insulator charges cannot flow, only shift.
This shift is polarization.
It explains why balloons stick to walls.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): The nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes, so a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Why does a charged balloon on a wall fall after a while?
o: Charge leaks away through the air and wall
questions.w: Moist air and surfaces slowly drain charge.
sol: Charge is not permanent on an insulator in air.
Water vapor lets it leak.
Less charge means weaker attraction, so gravity wins.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): The nearer opposite charge pulls harder than the farther like charge pushes, so a charged balloon sticks to a neutral wall.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Why does a pointed lightning rod help protect a building?
o: Charge concentrates at points, bleeding off gently or giving lightning a safe path to ground
It attracts no charge at all
questions.w: Sharp points concentrate field and lead charge safely to ground.
sol: Charge crowds at sharp points.
A conducting path to ground carries the current away.
This keeps it from going through the building.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A car is hit by lightning. Why are the passengers usually safe?
o: Charge flows along the metal outside, and the field inside is near zero
Rubber tires insulate the car from the strike
questions.w: A conducting shell shields its inside.
sol: Charge spreads on the outer surface.
The field inside a conductor shell is about zero.
Tires alone cannot stop a lightning strike.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Match each charging process to its description.
pairs: Electrons move between two rubbed materials
Touching shares charge, giving the same sign
Charge separated by a nearby rod and then grounded
Charges in an insulator shift, with no net change
questions.w: Four ways to move or rearrange charge.
sol: Friction transfers electrons.
Conduction needs contact.
Induction needs grounding; polarization leaves net charge zero.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Put the steps of safely handling a static-sensitive chip in order.
items: Put on a wrist strap connected to ground
Take the chip out of its antistatic bag
Place the chip in the socket
questions.w: Ground yourself before touching the chip.
sol: Drain your own charge first.
Work on a grounded mat.
Only then handle the chip.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Distance between two charges is halved. The force becomes:
questions.w: Force ∝ 1/r².
sol: So 4 times larger.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Charges 1.5 µC and 2.5 µC are 3.0 cm apart. Find the force in newtons. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: Convert cm to m before squaring.
sol: ≈ 37 N; forgetting to convert gives a nonsense number.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Two charges exert 9.0 N on each other at 0.10 m. At what distance would the force be 1.0 N? Answer in meters.
questions.w: Force ∝ 1/r².
sol: Force drops by 9.
So distance rises by √9 = 3.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A 40 N force acts at distance r. Charge 1 triples, charge 2 is halved, and the distance doubles. New force in newtons?
questions.w: Multiply the factors.
sol: Charges: 3 × ½ = 1.5.
Distance: 1/2² = 1/4.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Distance tripled and both charges doubled. The new force is:
questions.w: Charges give 2 × 2 = 4; distance gives 1/9.
sol: F ∝ q₁q₂/r².
Factor = (2×2)/3².
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: q₁ is halved, q₂ is tripled, and the distance is halved. The force becomes:
questions.w: Factor = (½ × 3)/(½)².
sol: Charges: ½ × 3 = 3/2.
Distance: 1/(½)² = 4.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A +4q sphere and a +q sphere repel. Which statement is right?
o: The forces on the two spheres are equal in size and opposite in direction
The +4q sphere feels 4 times more force
The +q sphere feels 4 times more force
Only the smaller sphere feels a force
questions.w: Newton's third law: they act on each other with equal forces.
sol: Coulomb's force is mutual.
Each charge's field acts on the other.
Bigger charge does not mean bigger force on it.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Two identical-mass balls on strings repel; one has charge +4q, the other +q. Both hang at rest. Compared with each other, the string angles are:
o: the +4q ball hangs at a larger angle
the +q ball hangs at a larger angle

They move up, so the leaves hold less charge.

questions.q: A positive rod is brought near a neutral metal sphere on an insulator. The sphere is grounded briefly, then the ground is removed, then the rod is removed. The sphere is now:

questions.q: Two identical positive charges are fixed. Along the line between them, where could a third negative charge feel zero net force?

Only at the midpoint are distances equal.
So net force is zero only there.

questions.q: A +q and a −q are fixed 1 m apart. On the straight line through them, where can a small positive test charge feel zero net force?
questions.w: Between them the forces add; outside, the nearer charge always wins.
sol: At the midpoint both forces point the same way, so they add.
Outside, the nearer charge exerts the stronger force.
The charges are equal in size, so they never cancel.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): Field lines point away from + and toward −, in the direction of force on a positive test charge.

questions.q: At the midpoint between +q and −q, the electric field points:
o: toward −q, and is twice one charge's field
questions.w: Both fields point the same way there.
sol: +q pushes away from itself.
−q pulls toward itself.
Same direction, so they add.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): Field lines point away from + and toward −, in the direction of force on a positive test charge.

questions.q: At the midpoint between two equal positive charges, the electric field is:
questions.w: The two fields point in opposite directions with equal size.
sol: Each pushes away from itself.
At the midpoint the pushes are opposite.
Equal sizes cancel.

questions.q: A charged comb picks up a bit of paper. Soon the paper jumps off. Why?
o: It gained the comb's charge by contact, so it is repelled
questions.w: Polarization first, then conduction.
sol: Polarization attracted the paper.
Contact shared some charge.
Now the same sign, so repulsion.

questions.q: Why do paint droplets from an electrostatic sprayer spread out evenly and coat the object's back?
o: Droplets have like charge so they repel; the grounded object attracts them
questions.w: Like charges repel; opposite (or induced) attract.
sol: Droplets all carry the same sign.
So they spread apart.
The object attracts them, even to its back.
From your notes · Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii): Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.

questions.q: A wrist strap for electronics work has a 1 MΩ resistor in it. Why is that resistor there?
o: To limit current if the wearer touches a live circuit
To build up charge on the wearer
To speed up discharge to zero seconds
To make the strap a perfect insulator
questions.w: It still drains static slowly but limits dangerous current.
sol: Static charge is tiny and drains fine through 1 MΩ.
A direct wire would be a shock hazard.
So the resistor keeps it safe.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Select ALL true statements about a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium.
o: Excess charge is on the surface
Field lines meet the surface at right angles
Charge spreads perfectly evenly on every shape
questions.w: Charge crowds at sharp points, so it is not uniform.
sol: Free charges stop moving when the field inside is zero.
They sit on the surface; the field at the surface is perpendicular.
On pointed shapes charge is denser at the tips.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Select ALL actions that reduce static buildup.
o: Walking on carpet in rubber-soled shoes
questions.w: Rubber-soled shoes on carpet help build charge.
sol: Moist air drains charge.
Grounding paths drain it directly.
Rubber on carpet insulates and charges you.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A 3.0 nC point charge. Use E = F/q with Coulomb's law to find the field at 0.30 m from it, in N/C. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: E = kq/r².
sol: Place a test charge q₀ there: F = kqq₀/r².
E = F/q₀ = kq/r².
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A 1.0 mA current flows for 3.2 ms. How many electrons pass a point? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.w: Q = It, then N = Q/e.
sol: N = Q/e.
≈ 2.0×10¹³ electrons.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Air breaks down and sparks when the field reaches about 3×10⁶ V/m. About how many volts across a 1.0 mm gap before a spark? (field × gap)
questions.w: V = E × d.
sol: Convert 1.0 mm to 0.0010 m.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A rod loses 3.0×10¹² electrons. What is its charge in µC? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C; give the magnitude)
questions.w: Q = ne.
sol: Losing electrons leaves the rod positive.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Two equal charges repel with 0.90 N at 0.10 m. Find each charge, in µC. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: q² = Fr²/k.
sol: F = kq²/r², so q² = Fr²/k.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Two +2.0 µC charges repel with 0.20 N. How far apart are they, in meters? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: r² = kq₁q₂/F.
sol: Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: +8.0 µC and −2.0 µC identical spheres attract. They touch and are returned to 0.30 m apart. What is the new force in newtons? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: Total charge splits evenly after touching.
sol: Total = +6.0 µC, so each sphere has +3.0 µC.
Now they repel.

questions.q: Identical spheres of −10 µC and +6.0 µC touch and are separated. What is the charge on each, in µC?
questions.w: Total is conserved and shared.
sol: Split between two identical spheres.
−2.0 µC each.

questions.q: Sphere A has charge Q. It touches identical neutral sphere B, is separated, then touches identical neutral sphere C. What fraction of Q does A end with? (decimal)
questions.w: Each touch splits A's charge in half.
sol: After B: Q/2.
After C: half of Q/2.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: An electron (m = 9.11×10⁻³¹ kg) sits in a field of 2.0×10³ N/C. What is its acceleration in m/s²? (e = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.w: F = eE, a = F/m.
sol: ≈ 3.5×10¹⁴ m/s²: huge, since electrons are so light.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A −2.0 µC charge sits between +4.0 µC (0.20 m to its left) and +1.0 µC (0.30 m to its right). Find the net force magnitude in newtons. (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: Both attract, in opposite directions.
sol: Opposite directions, so subtract: ≈ 1.6 N toward the +4.0 µC.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: A +2.0 µC charge sits midway between +4.0 µC and +1.0 µC charges 0.60 m apart. What is the net force in newtons? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: Both repel; the pushes oppose.
sol: Each distance is 0.30 m.
Pushes: 0.80 N and 0.20 N in opposite directions.
Net ≈ 0.60 N toward the +1.0 µC charge.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Charges +4q and +q are 0.90 m apart. How far from the +4q is the point on the line between them where the net field is zero? (meters)
questions.w: Equal fields: 4/x² = 1/(d−x)².
sol: Set 4kq/x² = kq/(0.90−x)².
Take square roots: 2(0.90−x) = x.
x = 0.60 m from +4q.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: +4.0 µC and −1.0 µC are 0.50 m apart. On the line beyond the −1.0 µC (away from the +4.0 µC), where is the net field zero? Give the distance from the −1.0 µC in meters.
questions.w: Equal and opposite fields: 4/(0.5+x)² = 1/x².
sol: Zero-field point lies on the weaker-charge side, outside.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

questions.q: Three +3.0 µC charges sit at corners of a right angle: one at the corner, one 0.30 m along x, one 0.30 m along y. What is the net force magnitude on the corner charge in newtons? (k = 8.99×10⁹)
questions.w: Add the two perpendicular forces as vectors.
sol: They are at right angles.

sol: Need F × 2.
r factor = 1/√2.

questions.w: F ∝ 1/r².

r² = 9.

questions.q: Two identical hollow metal spheres carry +10 µC and −2 µC. They touch and are separated. Compared with before, the force between them at the same distance:
o: stays attractive and is the same
questions.w: After touching each has +4 µC.
sol: Total +8 µC, so +4 µC each.
Both are now positive.
So they repel.

o: the same as if Q were alone, pointing outward

sol: Inner surface gets −Q.
Outer surface gets +Q.
Outside, the field looks like Q alone.
Notes|n3|Charge, fields and static electricity (area ii)

o: The sphere is attracted even though it has no net charge
questions.w: Induction/polarization puts opposite charge nearer.
sol: Nearer −charge pulls harder than the farther +charge pushes.
Net force is attraction.
No net charge was added.

outside, closer to the larger (+3q) charge

Outside near −q: nearer balances the smaller size.

Flowing fuel and clothing add charge.

Straight line through 0 means F ∝ 1/r².
This is Coulomb's inverse-square law.

questions.q: A signal repeats 10 times every second (10 Hz). How long does one cycle take, in milliseconds?

questions.w: T = 1/f, then convert seconds to ms.
sol: Multiply by 1000 to change seconds to milliseconds: 40 ms.
Common slip: leaving the answer in seconds.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A signal has a frequency of 60 Hz. Find its period in milliseconds.
questions.w: T = 1/f; US mains cycle takes about 16.7 ms.
sol: In ms: 16.7 ms.
Memory hook: 60 Hz is about 16.7 ms, 50 Hz is exactly 20 ms.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: An oscilloscope shows one full cycle lasting 8 ms. What is the frequency in hertz?
questions.w: Frequency is 1 divided by period, so a short period means a high frequency.
sol: Change 8 ms to 0.008 s.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: What is the unit of frequency? (one word)
questions.w: Hertz means cycles per second.
sol: Frequency counts cycles each second.
One cycle per second is 1 hertz (Hz).
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A sine wave has a peak voltage of 170 V. What is its peak-to-peak voltage?
questions.w: Peak-to-peak spans from the top peak to the bottom peak, so it is twice the peak.
sol: Peak is measured from zero to the top.
Peak-to-peak goes from −170 V to +170 V.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: Wall power is 120 V RMS. What is its peak voltage? Give your answer to the nearest volt.
questions.w: Peak is about 1.414 times the RMS value.
sol: RMS is the DC-equivalent heating value, always smaller than the peak.
V_peak = V_rms × √2.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A 12 Ω heating element runs on 120 V RMS. How much power does it use?
questions.w: RMS voltage works in P = V²/R just like DC voltage.
sol: RMS was defined to give the same heating as DC.
So use P = V²/R with V = 120 V.
P = 14400 ÷ 12 = 1200 W. Do not use 170 V peak here.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: On an oscilloscope a sine wave goes from +8 V to −8 V (16 V peak-to-peak). Find its RMS voltage.
questions.w: Convert peak-to-peak to peak first, then divide by √2.
sol: Peak-to-peak 16 V means peak = 16 ÷ 2 = 8 V.
V_rms = V_peak ÷ √2.
8 ÷ 1.414 = 5.66 V. Common error: dividing 16 by √2.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: An oscilloscope is set to 2 ms per division. One full cycle spans 5 divisions. Find the frequency in hertz.
questions.w: Time per cycle = divisions × time per division; frequency is its inverse.
sol: Period = 5 × 2 ms = 10 ms = 0.010 s.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A sine voltage with a 12 V peak is applied to a 6 Ω resistor. What is the average power? (Use RMS.)
questions.w: Average power uses RMS, not peak, because the voltage spends time near zero.
sol: P = V_rms² ÷ R = 72 ÷ 6 = 12 W.
Using the peak gives 24 W, twice too big, because the peak only lasts an instant.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: An ideal transformer steps 120 V down to 12 V. The 12 V side supplies a 5 A load. What current flows in the 120 V side?
questions.w: An ideal transformer passes power through unchanged: lower voltage means higher current on that side.
sol: Secondary power = 12 V × 5 A = 60 W.
Ideal means input power = output power = 60 W.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A transformer has 100 turns on its primary and 500 turns on its secondary. The primary gets 120 V AC. What is the secondary voltage?
questions.w: Voltage is proportional to turns, so more secondary turns steps voltage up.
sol: Voltage ratio = turns ratio = 500 ÷ 100 = 5.
Transformers only work on AC, because a changing field is needed.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: Which quantity does an ideal transformer NOT change between its input and output?
questions.w: The magnetic field alternates at the supply frequency, so the output cycles at the same rate.
sol: A transformer changes voltage and current in opposite directions.
The magnetic field in the core is driven by the input AC, so output repeats at the same rate.
60 Hz in means 60 Hz out.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A power line must deliver 10 kW. The line wires total 2 Ω. If it is sent at 2000 V, how many watts are lost heating the wires?
questions.w: Find the line current first, then use I²R.
sol: Loss = I²R = 25 × 2 = 50 W.
At 200 V the current would be 50 A and loss would be 5000 W, half the power.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A 12 V DC source and an AC source with 12 V RMS are each connected to identical resistors. Compared with the DC resistor, the AC resistor gets:
questions.w: RMS is defined so that it gives the same average heating as DC of that voltage.
sol: RMS = the DC value that heats equally.
Current direction does not matter for heating, since I²R is always positive.
So 12 V RMS AC heats like 12 V DC.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A meter set to AC volts is placed between the hot slot and the neutral slot of a working US outlet. It reads about:
questions.w: Hot-to-neutral is the full supply, shown as the RMS value.
sol: The hot wire swings about the neutral voltage.
A meter reads RMS by default: about 120 V.
170 V is the peak, which a normal meter does not display.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A lamp switch is wired into the hot wire rather than the neutral wire. Why is this safer?
o: With the switch off, the lamp socket is not at 120 V
It turns the AC into DC
questions.w: A switch in the hot leg removes the 120 V from everything after it.
sol: Neutral is near 0 V; hot is the live one.
If the switch opened the neutral, the lamp would still be connected to hot.
Someone touching the socket could then be shocked.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A frayed hot wire touches the metal case of a toaster, which has a ground wire. What does the ground wire do?
o: Gives the fault a low-resistance path so the breaker trips
Lowers the case voltage by raising resistance
Carries the toaster's normal current back
questions.w: Ground is only a safety path. It makes a big fault current so the breaker opens fast.
sol: The hot wire shorts to the case.
Case is bonded to ground, so a large current flows and the breaker trips.
Normal return current goes in the neutral wire, not ground.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): US outlet: hot (black, ≈120 V RMS to ground), neutral (white, return path, ≈0 V), ground (green or bare, fault path only).

questions.q: How many diodes does a full-wave bridge rectifier use? (number)
questions.w: A bridge uses four diodes so both halves of the AC cycle give current in one direction.

Four are arranged in a diamond (bridge).

questions.q: A US full-wave rectifier works on 60 Hz mains. How many output pulses are produced each second?
questions.w: A full-wave rectifier flips the negative half cycles, so it gives two pulses per cycle.
sol: Each AC cycle has one positive and one negative half.
Full-wave uses both halves.
2 × 60 = 120 pulses per second (a half-wave gives 60).

questions.q: Dry skin may have a resistance near 100 kΩ. How much current flows if 120 V is placed across it?

sol: That is only just felt. Wet skin has far lower resistance, so the current is much greater.

questions.q: Assume wet hands give a body resistance of 1500 Ω. How much current flows from 120 V through the body? Answer in mA.
questions.w: Wet skin means low resistance, so the same voltage pushes a dangerous current.
sol: That is 80 mA.
Over 100 mA across the chest can cause fibrillation, so 80 mA is in the danger zone. Voltage is the push; current does the harm.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): Voltage drives that current through body resistance; wet skin means lower resistance.

questions.q: Four lemon cells (copper and steel) are connected in series. Each gives about 0.7 V. What is the total voltage?

sol: Each cell is a copper plate, a steel plate and acid juice.
Series: add the voltages.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: Why does a lemon with a copper strip and a steel strip make a voltage?
o: Two different metals in an electrolyte react differently
The lemon is a tiny AC generator
The lemon stores charge like a capacitor
Copper and steel are both magnets
questions.w: A battery needs two unlike metals and a conducting liquid.
sol: The acid juice is the electrolyte.
The two metals react differently with it, so one gains electrons and one loses them.
Two strips of the same metal would give about 0 V.

questions.q: Two 1.5 V AA cells, each rated 2000 mAh, are connected in parallel. What is the total capacity in mAh?

Each cell supplies half the current, so the pack lasts twice as long.

questions.q: Two parallel strings each have three 1.5 V, 2000 mAh cells in series. The strings are joined in parallel. The pack is:
questions.w: Series adds voltage. Parallel adds capacity.

Two identical strings in parallel: voltage stays 4.5 V, capacity doubles to 4000 mAh.
Do the series step and the parallel step separately.

questions.q: A 9 V battery holds 500 mAh. A circuit draws a steady 25 mA. About how many hours will the battery last?

Time = 500 mAh ÷ 25 mA.

questions.q: A 3.0 V battery holds 2000 mAh. How much energy is stored? Answer in watt-hours.

= 6 Wh.

questions.q: A 1000 W heater made for 230 V is plugged into 120 V instead. Assuming its resistance stays the same, about how much power does it use?

questions.q: A 120 V RMS, 60 Hz outlet has v = 170 sin(2π·60·t). What is the instantaneous voltage at t = 2.0 ms? Give your answer in volts.

questions.q: A 50 Hz sine wave crosses zero going up at t = 0. When does it first reach its peak? Answer in ms.

questions.q: A 10 V peak sine wave and a 10 V DC source are connected to identical resistors. The AC resistor's average power compared with the DC one is:

questions.q: Select ALL statements that are true about AC power in a US home.
o: The voltage reverses direction 120 times each second

The 120 V rating is an RMS value
The current always flows one way
The neutral wire is the dangerous live wire

questions.q: Put these in order for electric power going from a power plant to a wall outlet.

Step down near the home to 120 V.

questions.q: Match each wire in a US outlet to its job.
