questions.q: A car battery with liquid acid inside is called a:
questions.w: A wet cell uses a liquid electrolyte.
sol: Lead-acid car batteries contain liquid.
Dry cells use paste, such as alkaline AA cells.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): Dry cell = paste electrolyte (alkaline, zinc-carbon); wet cell = liquid electrolyte (lead-acid).
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: A 60 W bulb runs on 120 V. How much current does it draw?
questions.w: Use I = P ÷ V.
sol: Power = voltage × current.
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: Which is a typical reason AC is used for the power grid instead of DC?
o: Transformers can easily change AC voltage
AC does not heat the wires
questions.w: Transformers only work with changing current, and they let us pick the best voltage for each job.
sol: High voltage cuts line current and loss.
Low voltage is safer in the home.
Transformers do both easily with AC.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): UsesElectronics, LEDs, motors on batteriesPower distribution (transformers easily change voltage)
Notes|n4|DC and AC (area iii)

questions.q: Which switch simply makes or breaks one path, with one pole and one throw?
questions.w: SPST is the plain on/off switch.
sol: S = single pole, T = throw.
One moving contact and one path: SPST.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): SPST switchOne pole, one throw: simple on/off
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: How many terminals does a standard SPDT switch have?
questions.w: One common terminal plus two outputs.
sol: Single pole: one common.
Double throw: two positions, each with an output terminal.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: How many terminals does a standard DPDT switch have?
questions.w: A DPDT is two SPDT switches moved by one handle.
sol: Each pole has one common and two outputs (3 terminals).
Two poles give 2 × 3 = 6.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A small 5 V signal needs to turn on a 120 V lamp. Which device lets the small signal control the lamp while keeping the circuits separate?
questions.w: A relay uses a coil to move contacts, so the control side and load side are not connected.
sol: The coil is the small control circuit.
The magnetic field closes contacts in the separate lamp circuit.
A fuse only protects and a GFCI only detects leaks.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A diode is put across a relay coil to stop a voltage spike when the coil is switched off. How should it be connected?
o: Cathode (stripe) to the positive side of the coil
Anode (plain end) to the positive side of the coil
In series with the coil, forward biased
Across the contacts instead of the coil
questions.w: The diode must be reverse-biased during normal operation so it only conducts during the spike.
sol: During normal use the supply pushes current through the coil, so the diode should block.
When the switch opens the collapsing field reverses the coil voltage.
Then the diode conducts and absorbs the energy. The stripe (cathode) goes to the + side.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Add a reverse diode across the coil.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: Why does a relay coil make a high-voltage spike when its current is switched off?
o: The collapsing magnetic field forces the current to keep flowing
questions.w: A coil resists a change in current. Cutting power makes its field collapse and induces a voltage.
sol: A coil stores energy in its magnetic field.
Cutting the current quickly makes the field collapse quickly.
The fast collapse induces a large voltage that can damage a transistor or switch.
From your notes · Magnetism and induction (adjacent): Ørsted: current makes a magnetic field.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A lamp is wired through the normally closed (NC) contact of a relay. What happens when the coil is energized?
questions.w: Energizing the coil moves the common contact from NC to NO.
sol: At rest, NC touches the common, so the lamp is on.
Coil power pulls the armature away from NC.
The circuit through NC opens and the lamp goes off.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A relay coil has a resistance of 300 Ω and is powered by 12 V. How much coil current flows, in mA?
questions.w: The coil is just a resistor as far as DC current goes.
sol: Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A relay has contacts rated 10 A at 120 V. Which load can it safely switch?
questions.w: Compare each load's current (P ÷ V) with the 10 A contact rating.
sol: 1000 W ÷ 120 V = 8.3 A, which is under 10 A.
1500 W gives 12.5 A, 1800 W gives 15 A and 2400 W gives 20 A.
Those would overheat or weld the contacts.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A microcontroller pin can supply only about 20 mA, but a relay coil needs 70 mA. What is the usual fix?
o: Use a transistor to drive the coil
Connect the coil directly to the pin
Put a fuse in series with the pin
Use a bigger diode across the pin
questions.w: The pin controls a transistor, and the transistor carries the larger coil current.
sol: 70 mA is more than the pin can give.
A small current into the transistor's base lets it switch the larger coil current.
The flyback diode still goes across the coil.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A 1200 W hair dryer runs on 120 V. Which is the smallest standard fuse (5, 10, 15, 20 A) that will not blow? Answer in amps.
questions.w: Find the current, then pick a rating at or above it.
sol: A fuse rated exactly 10 A is enough in this question's rule: at or above.
(Real installs often leave extra margin, but use the rule given.)
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Fuse size: I = P/V, then choose the smallest standard rating at or above I.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A 300 W load runs on 12 V. Which is the smallest standard fuse (10, 20, 25, 30, 40 A) that will not blow? Answer in amps.
questions.w: The current is much bigger at low voltage.
sol: 25 A is available, so choose 25 A (at or above 25).
Low-voltage circuits need high current for the same power.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A circuit uses 14 AWG wire, which is rated for 15 A. A person swaps the 15 A fuse for a 30 A fuse. What is the danger?
o: The wire can overheat without the fuse blowing
The fuse will blow more often
The load will get less current
questions.w: A fuse protects the wire. A fuse that is too big lets too much current flow.
sol: The wire gets hot when current is above its rating.
A 30 A fuse still carries 20 A without blowing.
The wire insulation could melt and cause a fire.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A 1000 W heater, an 800 W toaster and 400 W of lamps all run on one 120 V circuit. What is the total current in amps?
questions.w: Loads in parallel add their currents, which is the same as adding their power.
sol: ≈ 18.3 A. That trips a 15 A breaker.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: Why does plugging more appliances into one outlet circuit make the breaker more likely to trip?
o: Appliances are in parallel, so their currents add
Appliances are in series, so their voltages add
questions.w: Home loads are connected in parallel across 120 V, so each draws its own current.
sol: Each appliance adds its own current.
The total current in the wire is the sum.
When the sum goes above the breaker rating, it trips.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A GFCI sees 8.020 A leaving on the hot wire and 8.000 A returning on the neutral. What happens?
o: Nothing, because the current is under 15 A
The GFCI trips only if the difference is over 1 A
questions.w: A GFCI compares outgoing and returning current. A 20 mA gap means current is leaking somewhere else.
sol: A GFCI trips at about 5 mA of difference.
The missing current may be going through a person.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: Where do building codes require GFCI protection?
o: Near water, such as bathrooms and outdoors
questions.w: Wet places raise the chance of current passing through a person to ground.
sol: Water lowers body resistance.
GFCIs cut the power within milliseconds of a leak.
So they are used by sinks, bathrooms, outdoors.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A person with wet skin (about 2000 Ω) touches a 120 V hot wire and ground. How much current flows, in mA?
questions.w: Use Ohm's law for the body path.
sol: A GFCI would trip at 5 mA; a 15 A breaker would not trip at all.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): US outlet: hot (black, ≈120 V RMS to ground), neutral (white, return path, ≈0 V), ground (green or bare, fault path only).
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A three-way circuit has the lamp ON. You flip switch A, then switch B, then switch A again. The lamp is now:
questions.w: Every flip of either switch changes the lamp state.
sol: Start on.
Flip A: off. Flip B: on. Flip A: off.
Three flips (an odd number) leave it changed from the start: off.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: To control one hallway lamp from THREE places, which switch set is correct?
o: Two SPDT switches at the ends and one DPDT wired as a crossover in the middle
Two DPDT switches at the ends only
questions.w: The middle switch must swap the two traveler wires, which is a DPDT wired crossed.
sol: End switches are SPDT (3-way).
The middle one swaps which traveler goes where, so it is a DPDT wired crossed.
Each flip then still toggles the lamp.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A lamp should light only when a door switch AND a key switch are both closed. How should they be wired?
o: In a loop around the lamp
questions.w: Series switches give AND logic.
sol: Current must pass through both.
Open either, and the path breaks.
Parallel would give OR.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Switch logic: switches in series = AND (both closed to light).
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A lamp must light when (A and B) are closed, OR when C is closed. Which wiring does this?
o: A in series with B, and that branch in parallel with C
A, B and C all in series
A, B and C all in parallel
A in parallel with B, and that pair in series with C
questions.w: Series is AND, parallel is OR.
sol: A and B need to both be closed: series.
Either that branch or C: parallel.
So (A series B) parallel C.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: How many separate circuits can a DPDT switch control at the same time?
questions.w: A DPDT has two poles, which are moved together.
sol: Each pole is an independent moving contact.
Two poles = two circuits.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A circuit breaker's bimetal strip bends and trips the breaker when it is hot. Why does it bend?
o: The two metals expand by different amounts
The strip melts at one end
Magnetism pulls it away from the contact
questions.w: Two bonded metals expand at different rates, so the strip curves when heated.
sol: Overcurrent heats the strip.
One metal grows more than the other.
The curve pushes a latch that opens the contacts.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A breaker has both a thermal part and a magnetic part. Which statement is right?
o: Magnetic reacts fast to very large short-circuit current; thermal reacts slowly to small overloads
Thermal reacts fast to shorts; magnetic reacts to slow overloads
Both react only after one minute
Only the magnetic part can be reset
questions.w: Big surges need an instant trip; mild overloads need time to heat the strip.
sol: A short circuit makes huge current in an instant, and a coil's strong field trips it at once.
A 20% overload heats the strip slowly, so it trips later.
Together they cover both cases.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Circuit breakerTrips on overcurrent (heat bends a bimetal strip; a coil handles big shorts); resettable
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A motor runs at 3 A but draws about 18 A for 0.2 s at startup. Which fuse is the best choice?
questions.w: A slow-blow fuse ignores a brief surge but still opens on a lasting overload.
sol: Running current 3 A means a 5 A rating gives a small margin.
A fast-blow 5 A would open on the 18 A surge.
Slow-blow rides through 0.2 s.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A new fuse blows right away after replacing a blown fuse of the same rating. What is the most likely cause?
o: A short circuit or overload is still present
The fuse was too small, so use a bigger one
questions.w: A fuse is a sign, not the problem. The fault must be found and fixed.
sol: Blowing again means the current is still too high.
A bigger fuse would hide the problem and risk a fire.
Unplug loads and look for a short.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: Put the steps of a relay turning on in order.
items: Control circuit sends current to the coil
The coil makes a magnetic field
The armature is pulled toward the coil
questions.w: Relays turn a small electrical signal into motion and then into a switched circuit.
sol: Current flows in the coil.
The field attracts the armature.
The contacts touch and the load turns on.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: a moving contact that is switched
a position or path the contact can reach
open when the relay is at rest
closed when the relay is at rest
questions.w: Switch names count poles and throws.
sol: Poles are the switched circuits.
Throws are the choices.
NO and NC describe the rest state.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: Select ALL devices that open a circuit when current goes above a set value.
questions.w: Fuses and breakers respond to overcurrent.
sol: A relay switches by a coil signal.
A DPDT switch is moved by hand.
A GFCI responds to imbalance (leakage), not size of current.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A 15 A breaker is on a 240 V circuit. What is the largest power it can carry before it trips, in watts?
questions.w: Power = voltage × current.
sol: P = V × I.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A SPDT switch has its common wired to the supply, and each of the other two terminals to a different lamp. Which result is correct?
o: Exactly one lamp is on at a time
Both lamps are off in the middle
questions.w: The common connects to only one output at any time.
sol: The common touches either terminal 1 or terminal 2.
So current goes to one lamp.
The other lamp is off.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): The commons go to the source (switch 1) and the lamp (switch 2); two traveler wires join the other terminals.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: A lamp's switch is wired in the neutral wire instead of the hot wire. With the switch OFF, a person touches the metal socket thread. What is the problem?
o: The socket is still connected to hot and can shock
Nothing, since the lamp is off
questions.w: The switch must break the hot connection to make the socket safe.
sol: Neutral switch off leaves hot wire going to the socket.
Hot is at 120 V to ground.
A person touching it and ground gets a shock path, even though the lamp is off.
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: In what unit is a fuse rating given? (one word)
questions.w: A fuse rating is a current limit.
sol: Fuses melt when current is too high.
Current is in amperes (amps).
Notes|n8|Control devices (area vi)

questions.q: To measure the current in a circuit, the meter is connected:
o: In series, so the current goes through the meter
Across the battery with no load
questions.w: An ammeter counts the charge that passes through it, so it must be in the path.
sol: Break the circuit at one point.
Put the meter in the gap.
In parallel, an ammeter acts like a short.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: To measure the voltage across a resistor, the meter is connected:
questions.w: A voltmeter measures the difference between two points, so touch its probes to both ends.
sol: Voltage is measured across a part.
The meter has very high resistance, so it barely changes the circuit.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: On most multimeters, the black probe goes into which jack?
questions.w: COM means common and is the reference for all readings.
sol: Black always plugs in COM.
The red probe moves between the other jacks depending on what is measured.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A resistor has color bands brown, black, red, then gold. What is its value in ohms?
questions.w: The first two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier. Gold is a 5% tolerance.
sol: Brown = 1, black = 0.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A resistor has color bands yellow, violet, orange, gold. What is its value in kΩ?
questions.w: Digits 4 and 7, then ×1000.
sol: Yellow = 4, violet = 7.
Orange = ×1000.
From your notes · Units, formulas, resistor code: Examples: orange-orange-brown-gold = 330 Ω ±5%; yellow-violet-red-gold = 4.7 kΩ ±5%.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A resistor has color bands red, red, brown, gold. What is its value in ohms?
questions.w: Red is 2 and brown multiplies by 10.
sol: Red red = 22.
Brown = ×10.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A resistor is orange, orange, yellow, gold (5%). What is the lowest value it could really be, in kΩ?
questions.w: Read the nominal value, then subtract the tolerance.
sol: Orange orange = 33, yellow = ×10,000, so 330 kΩ.
Gold means ±5%, so the lowest is 95% of 330.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A red LED needs 15 mA and drops 2.0 V. It runs from a 9 V battery with a series resistor. What resistance is needed, in Ω?
questions.w: The resistor must drop whatever voltage the LED does not.
sol: Resistor voltage = 9 − 2.0 = 7.0 V.
≈ 467 Ω. A standard 470 Ω would be used.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 100 Ω resistor has 12 V across it. Which is the smallest power rating that is safe?
questions.w: Heat in the resistor is P = V²/R. The rating must be above that.
sol: 1/4, 1/2 and 1 W resistors would overheat.
The smallest listed rating above 1.44 W is 2 W.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Two resistors, 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ, are in series with a 9 V battery. What is the voltage across the 2 kΩ resistor?
questions.w: In a series circuit the voltage is shared in proportion to resistance.
sol: Total R = 3 kΩ.
V = 3 mA × 2 kΩ = 6 V.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: On a breadboard, both legs of a resistor are pushed into the same 5-hole column. What does this do?
o: Shorts out the resistor so it does nothing
questions.w: Holes in one column are connected, so both ends of the part are the same node.
sol: Both leads touch the same metal strip.
Current can flow around the resistor through the strip.
A part with both ends on the same node has 0 V across it.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Why do ICs go across the center gap of a breadboard?
o: So pins on opposite sides are not connected
questions.w: The center gap splits the two halves, so each pin gets its own column.
sol: Each pin needs its own connection.
The gap isolates the two rows of pins.
Otherwise left and right pins would short.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A series circuit has a 9 V battery, a switch, resistor R1 and resistor R2. The lamp isn't lit. A voltmeter reads 9 V across R2 and 0 V across R1. What is the fault?
questions.w: In a series loop, an open part takes the whole supply voltage.
sol: No current flows, so there is no drop across good parts: R1 reads 0 V.
The open part has all 9 V across it.
The battery is fine, since 9 V is available.
From your notes · DC circuits, meters and faults (area v): A switch that is open has the full battery voltage across its terminals.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Three identical bulbs are in series on a battery. A wire is then connected across one bulb (shorting it). What happens to the other two?
questions.w: Shorting one bulb lowers the total resistance, so the current goes up.
sol: Total R drops from 3R to 2R.
I = V ÷ R rises by 1.5×.
More current through the two bulbs means more brightness.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A voltmeter is wrongly connected in series with a lamp and a 9 V battery. What do you see?
o: The meter reads nearly 9 V and the lamp stays dark
questions.w: A voltmeter has a huge resistance, so it takes almost all the voltage and lets almost no current pass.
sol: Meter resistance is millions of ohms.
The tiny current cannot light the lamp.
Almost all of 9 V drops across the meter, so it reads almost 9 V.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: What is a continuity test used to check?
o: Whether there is a low-resistance path between two points
questions.w: Continuity mode beeps if the path has very low resistance.
sol: Turn power off first.
Touch the probes to both ends of the wire or fuse.
A beep means a good, unbroken path.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A meter on a resistance range shows "OL" (or "1") while measuring a resistor. This usually means:
o: The resistance is above the range or the path is open
questions.w: OL means overload: the value is too large for that range.
sol: Try a higher range.
If it still shows OL, the part or wire may be open (broken).
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A meter shows 2.2 kΩ. What is this in ohms?
questions.w: k (kilo) means a thousand.
sol: Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Resistors of 220 Ω, 330 Ω and 470 Ω are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.w: Series resistances add.
sol: Add the three values.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Resistors of 100 Ω, 100 Ω and 50 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
questions.w: Parallel adds conductances (1/R).
sol: Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 100 Ω resistor is in series with two 200 Ω resistors in parallel, and then a 50 Ω resistor in series. What is the total resistance?
questions.w: Reduce the parallel part first, then add the series parts.
sol: Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Put these steps in order for measuring current safely in a powered circuit.
items: Break the circuit at one point
Set the meter to amps and move the red lead to the current jack
Connect the meter into the gap
Turn the power on and read
questions.w: A current meter must be placed in the path, so the circuit has to be opened first.
sol: Never open a live circuit.
Set the meter on the right range and jack before connecting.
Then power up and read.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 9 V battery powers an unknown resistor Rx in series with a 1 kΩ resistor. The voltage across the 1 kΩ is 3 V. What is Rx, in kΩ?
questions.w: Find the series current, then find Rx from its share of the voltage.
sol: I = 3 V ÷ 1 kΩ = 3 mA.
Voltage across Rx = 9 − 3 = 6 V.
Rx = 6 ÷ 3 mA = 2 kΩ.
From your notes · DC circuits, meters and faults (area v): Expand back: find the voltage across each group, then the current in each resistor (V = IR).
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Two LEDs in series each drop 2.0 V. They run at 10 mA from a 9 V battery. What series resistor is needed, in Ω?
questions.w: Subtract all the LED drops from the supply before using Ohm's law.
sol: LED drops: 2 × 2.0 = 4.0 V.
Resistor drop: 9 − 4 = 5 V.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Three red LEDs (about 2.0 V each) are in series with a resistor on a 5 V supply. What happens?
o: They do not light, since 6 V is needed
questions.w: The supply must exceed the sum of the LED drops.
sol: 5 V is less than 6 V.
Too little voltage for them to conduct, so no current flows.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: The longer leg of an LED is the:
questions.w: LEDs only work one way: current enters the anode.
sol: Long leg = +.
The flat spot on the case marks the cathode.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: What can happen if an LED is connected straight to a battery with no resistor?
o: It draws too much current and burns out
questions.w: An LED has almost no resistance once it conducts, so the resistor sets the current.
sol: Without a resistor, the current is limited only by the battery.
Too much current overheats the LED and destroys it.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Before changing wires in a circuit you are building, you should first:
questions.w: Do changes with the power off to avoid shorts and shocks.
sol: Wiring changes with power on can cause shorts.
Disconnect the battery first.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A battery you are using becomes hot while you wire a circuit. What is the best action?
o: Disconnect it and look for a short
questions.w: Heat means a large current, which could mean a short.
sol: Heat comes from high current through resistance.
A short can make a battery overheat.
Disconnect it, then fix the wiring.
From your notes · DC and AC (area iii): A short circuit (near-0 Ω path) gives huge current, heat, fire.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 12 V battery drives an 8 Ω resistor in series with a 16 Ω resistor. What power is used in the 8 Ω resistor, in watts?
questions.w: Find the current first, then use P = I²R.
sol: Total R = 24 Ω.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Match each meter setting to its use.
questions.w: Choosing the right setting is the first step of every measurement.
sol: Straight line means DC.
Wavy line means AC.
Ω is for resistance with the power off, A needs the meter in the path.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Select ALL steps that are correct when measuring a resistor that is in a circuit.
o: Lift one lead of the resistor out of the circuit
questions.w: The meter supplies its own test current, so the rest of the circuit must not interfere.
sol: Power off, so the battery doesn't change the reading.
Lift one leg so other parts in parallel are not measured.
Use the Ω setting.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A battery reads 9.0 V with nothing connected. With a 100 Ω load connected it reads 8.5 V. What is its internal resistance, in Ω?
questions.w: The missing voltage dropped across the battery's own resistance.
sol: Load current = 8.5 ÷ 100 = 0.085 A.
Lost voltage = 9.0 − 8.5 = 0.5 V.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A lamp has 12 V across it and 0.25 A through it. What is its resistance?
questions.w: Use Ohm's law R = V ÷ I.
sol: Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: How many ohms are in 1 MΩ?
questions.w: M (mega) means a million.
sol: Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: What unit is mAh a measure of?
questions.w: mAh = current × time, which is charge, not energy.
sol: Energy needs voltage too (Wh).
Trap: mAh is NOT energy.
Notes|n5|Current, voltage, resistance, power, energy (area iv)

questions.q: One joule per coulomb is the definition of which unit?
questions.w: Voltage is energy per charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.
sol: Voltage = energy ÷ charge.
1 A = 1 C/s and 1 W = 1 J/s are the other two.
Notes|n5|Current, voltage, resistance, power, energy (area iv)

questions.q: Convert 250 mA to amperes.
questions.w: Milli means ÷1000.

questions.q: A 120 V, 60 W bulb and a 120 V, 100 W bulb are wired in series across 120 V. Find the power in the 60 W bulb in watts.
questions.w: Find each resistance from R = V²/P, then the series current.
sol: P = I²R = 0.3125² × 240 = 23.4 W. The 60 W bulb is brighter in series, because the larger resistance gets more power.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 120 V circuit has a 15 A breaker. A 1500 W heater and a 600 W toaster are both plugged in (parallel). What total current do they draw?
questions.w: Powers add; I = P/V.
sol: Total power = 2100 W.
That is over 15 A, so the breaker trips.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Three 100 Ω, ¼ W resistors are in SERIES. What is the largest voltage across the whole string without exceeding any rating? Give volts.
questions.w: Each resistor can carry I = √(P/R) = 0.05 A.
sol: Safe current = √(0.25/100) = 50 mA.
String resistance = 300 Ω.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 100 Ω and a 400 Ω resistor, each rated ¼ W, are in PARALLEL. What is the largest total power the pair can dissipate without exceeding a rating? Give watts.
questions.w: Parallel means same voltage. The 100 Ω resistor reaches its limit first at 5 V.
sol: 400 Ω could take 10 V, so 5 V rules.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 12 V source feeds node A. From A, 100 Ω goes to P and 300 Ω goes to Q. From P, 200 Ω goes to ground; from Q, 100 Ω goes to ground. A 100 Ω resistor links P to Q. Find the current in the link, in amps (magnitude).
questions.w: Write KCL at P and at Q to find the two node voltages, then use Ohm's law on the link.
sol: Solve: Vp = 6.62 V, Vq = 4.55 V.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A balanced bridge: R1 = 120 Ω and R2 = 180 Ω form one side; R3 = 250 Ω and an unknown Rx form the other. The meter between the midpoints reads zero. Find Rx in ohms.
questions.w: Zero meter current means both dividers have the same ratio: R1/R2 = R3/Rx.
sol: Same midpoint voltage means same ratio.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, the resistor joining the two midpoints carries:
o: no current, so removing it changes nothing
the same current as the source
questions.w: Both midpoints sit at the same voltage, so nothing pushes current through the link.
sol: Balanced dividers give equal midpoint voltages.
No voltage difference means no current.
So you can take the link out or short it with no change.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 12 V battery has internal resistance 0.5 Ω and powers a 5.5 Ω lamp. A second identical 5.5 Ω lamp is added in PARALLEL. What is the battery's terminal voltage afterward? Give volts.
questions.w: More current means a bigger voltage drop inside the battery.
sol: Terminal V = 12 − 3.69 × 0.5 = 10.15 V, down from 11 V with one lamp.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A divider has two 10 kΩ resistors across 10 V. A voltmeter with 10 kΩ input resistance is placed across the lower resistor. What does it read? Give volts.
questions.w: The meter is in parallel with the lower resistor and loads it.
sol: 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ.
Not the 5 V you would expect: a real meter changes what it measures.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: An ammeter of 2 Ω resistance is inserted in series in a circuit of 10 V and 8 Ω. What current does it read? Give amps.
questions.w: The meter adds its own resistance to the loop.
sol: True current without the meter: 10/8 = 1.25 A.
With the meter: 10/(8 + 2) = 1.0 A.
So the meter reads 20% low.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 12 V source has internal resistance 6 Ω. Compare the power delivered to a 3 Ω load and to a 12 Ω load.
o: The 12 Ω load gets twice as much
questions.w: Two loads R1 and R2 give the same power when R1 × R2 = r². Here 3 × 12 = 6².
sol: Maximum power would come at 6 Ω, between the two.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A source has internal resistance 3 Ω and EMF 6 V. What is the maximum power it can deliver to any load? Give watts.
questions.w: Maximum power transfer happens when R_load = r.
sol: Load = 3 Ω, so total = 6 Ω.
P = I²R = 1 × 3 = 3 W. The other 3 W heats the source itself.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 12 V battery drives a 1 kΩ and a 3 kΩ resistor in series, with the 1 kΩ next to the battery's + terminal. Ground is the node BETWEEN the resistors. What is the voltage of the battery's negative terminal?
questions.w: Current is 3 mA. The 1 kΩ drops 3 V and the 3 kΩ drops 9 V. The negative terminal is 9 V below ground.
sol: Current = 12 V/4 kΩ = 3 mA.
Drops: 3 V across 1 kΩ, 9 V across 3 kΩ.
Ground is the middle node, so the + side is at +3 V and the − side is at −9 V.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Two 6 Ω resistors in series form a pair. That pair is in parallel with 3 Ω, and the combination is in series with 4 Ω. Find the total resistance in ohms.
questions.w: Reduce from the inside out.
sol: Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Rank these by power dissipated, largest first: 10 Ω across 12 V; 20 Ω across 12 V; 10 Ω and 20 Ω in series across 12 V; 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel across 12 V.
items: 10 Ω and 20 Ω in parallel across 12 V
10 Ω and 20 Ω in series across 12 V
questions.w: P = V²/R_eq, so smaller equivalent resistance means more power at the same voltage.
sol: Parallel pair: 6.67 Ω gives 21.6 W.
10 Ω gives 14.4 W; 20 Ω gives 7.2 W.
Series pair: 30 Ω gives 4.8 W.
From your notes · DC circuits, meters and faults (area v): Parallel bulbs: same voltage, so smaller R gets more power (P = V²/R).
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A lamp is shining normally on an ideal battery. Select ALL changes that would make it dimmer.
o: Add a resistor in series with the lamp
Swap the battery for a lower-voltage one
Add a second lamp in series
Add a second lamp in parallel with the first
questions.w: Dimmer means less current through the lamp. A parallel branch leaves the first lamp's voltage unchanged.
sol: Series resistance lowers the current.
Lower voltage lowers the current.
A second lamp in series adds resistance.
An ideal battery keeps its voltage, so a parallel lamp changes nothing for the first.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Bulb A is in series with a parallel pair B and C (all identical, ideal battery). Bulb C burns out (open). What happens to A and B?
o: A gets dimmer and B gets brighter
A and B both get brighter
A gets brighter and B gets dimmer
A and B stay the same
questions.w: Losing C leaves one path through B, so total resistance rises and current falls. B now carries all of it.
sol: Before: A carries I; B and C carry I/2 each.
After: total R rises (1.5 R to 2 R), so the current falls.
A has less current, so it dims. B now carries the full smaller current, which is bigger than before (I/2), so it brightens.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Two identical bulbs are in series on a battery. A wire is connected across bulb 1 only. Bulb 2 becomes:
questions.w: The wire shorts bulb 1, so bulb 2 alone sets the current and gets the full voltage.
sol: Bulb 1 has about 0 V across it, so it goes out.
Total resistance halves, so current doubles.
Bulb 2 has twice the voltage and twice the current, so it is brighter.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 6 V battery powers a 12 Ω, 24 Ω and 8 Ω resistor in parallel. How many watts does the battery supply in total?
questions.w: In parallel each resistor has 6 V, and the powers add.
sol: The source supplies the sum: 3 + 1.5 + 4.5 = 9 W.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 9 V battery feeds a 6 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. Find the power dissipated in the 3 Ω resistor in watts.
questions.w: Find the pair's voltage first, then P = V²/R.
sol: 6 ∥ 3 = 2 Ω; R_total = 8 Ω.
I = 9/8 A, so the pair has 9/8 × 2 = 2.25 V.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Three parallel branches carry 2 A, 3 A and an unknown current. The source supplies 8 A, and the voltage across every branch is 4 V. What is the unknown branch's resistance in ohms?
questions.w: KCL gives the missing branch current; then R = V/I.
sol: Parallel branch currents add: 8 = 2 + 3 + I.
I = 3 A.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A student wants to find a resistor's value from a voltmeter reading and an ammeter reading, and places the voltmeter across the resistor and ammeter together. What error is built in?
o: The voltmeter reads the resistor plus ammeter voltage, so R reads a little high
The ammeter reads the resistor current plus the voltmeter current, so R reads low
questions.w: The voltmeter spans both the resistor and the ammeter's tiny resistance, so the voltage is slightly too big.
sol: Ammeter is in series with the resistor and carries the true current.
Voltmeter reads V across resistor + ammeter.
R_measured = (V_R + V_A)/I, a bit larger than R.
From your notes · DC circuits, meters and faults (area v): Expand back: find the voltage across each group, then the current in each resistor (V = IR).
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: A 24 V source feeds two identical resistors in series. One resistor is then replaced by a wire (shorted), and the current rises from 2 A to what value in amps?
questions.w: Shorting one of two equal series resistors halves the total resistance.
sol: Before: R_total = 24/2 = 12 Ω, so each is 6 Ω.
After: only one 6 Ω remains.
Notes|n6|DC circuits, meters and faults (area v)

questions.q: Kirchhoff's current law rests on the conservation of which quantity?
questions.w: Charge cannot pile up at a node, so what flows in must flow out.
sol: KCL: current in = current out.
Current is charge per second, so equal current means equal charge.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Wire A brings 4 A into a junction. Wire B takes 1.5 A out. Wire C is the only other wire. How many amps leave through C?
questions.w: In = out: 4 = 1.5 + I.
sol: Charge in per second = charge out per second.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: KVL says voltage changes around a closed loop add to zero. This follows from conservation of:
questions.w: A charge that returns to its start has the same potential energy, so gains equal losses.
sol: Batteries raise its energy.
Resistors use it up.
Net change after a full loop = 0.
From your notes · Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals): KVL: the sum of voltage rises and drops around any closed loop = 0. (Energy is conserved.)
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: You trace a KVL loop through a resistor in the SAME direction as the current. The voltage change is:
questions.w: Conventional current runs from higher to lower potential through a resistor.
sol: Follow the current: potential falls.
Write −IR in the loop sum.
Against the current it would be +IR.
From your notes · Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals): A resistor is a drop in the direction of current; a source is a rise when you go through it from − to +.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: You guess a current's direction and your solution gives −2 A. This means:
o: the current really flows the other way, 2 A
the current is 2 A in your direction
questions.w: A negative sign only says the true direction is opposite to your arrow.
sol: Directions are guesses.
The size, 2 A, is still right.
Just reverse the arrow to fix the picture.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A node has three wires. 2 A flows in on one and 3 A flows in on another. The third wire carries:
questions.w: All the charge arriving must leave: 2 + 3 = 5 A.
sol: Nothing can build up at a node.
Currents in total 5 A.
So 5 A must leave.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A 14.4 V car alternator charges a 12 V battery (opposing) through 0.6 Ω in total. What is the charging current? Give amps.
questions.w: The net EMF drives current through the resistance.
sol: Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A jump-start joins a 12.6 V battery (0.02 Ω) to a dead 11 V battery (0.05 Ω) with cables of negligible resistance, + to + and − to −. What current flows in the loop? Give amps.
questions.w: One loop: net EMF divided by total resistance.
sol: Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Which is a correct KVL equation for one loop: a 10 V battery, 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series, clockwise current I?
questions.w: The battery is a rise (+10). Each resistor is a drop (−IR). The sum is zero.
sol: Rise: +10.
Drops: −2I and −3I.
Sum around the loop = 0, so I = 2 A.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Select ALL valid statements about KCL and KVL.
o: KCL applies at any node, even with batteries on the wires
KVL applies to any closed loop, even one with no battery
Counting current in as + and out as −, the sum at a node is zero
KVL says the current is the same everywhere in a loop
questions.w: KCL is about nodes and KVL is about loops. Neither says currents are equal everywhere.
sol: KCL holds at every node.
KVL holds around every closed loop.
Equal current is only true for a series path, not a law.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Match each law to what it says.
pairs: Currents in = currents out at a node
Voltage changes around a loop sum to zero
questions.w: Each law ties to a conservation idea or a component rule.
sol: Charge: KCL.
Energy: KVL and power balance.
Ohm's law relates one resistor's V and I.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Put the steps of the two-loop recipe in order.
items: Label a current and direction in each branch
Write KVL around two independent loops
Check power supplied equals power dissipated
questions.w: Set up unknowns, write independent equations, solve, then verify.
sol: Arrows first (wrong guesses just give negative answers).
KCL, then two KVL loops.
Solve, then check with power balance.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Node X has four wires: 3 A in, 5 A in, 2 A out, and an unknown wire carrying current OUT. How many amps is the unknown?
questions.w: In = out: 3 + 5 = 2 + I.
sol: Currents in: 8 A.
Currents out: 2 + I.
I = 6 A.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A 12 V source is across a 3 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. Find the current in the 3 Ω resistor of the pair. Give amps.
questions.w: Reduce, find the total current, then use the voltage across the pair.
sol: I = 12/5 = 2.4 A; voltage across the pair = 2.4 × 2 = 4.8 V.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A 20 V battery drives two resistors in series. One drops 7.5 V. What does the other drop? Give volts.
questions.w: KVL: the drops add up to the source voltage.
sol: Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: At a node, 4 A enters on wire 1 and 6 A enters on wire 2. Wire 3 carries 3 A out. How much must wire 4 carry?
questions.w: In = out. Total in is 10 A; wire 3 takes 3 A, so wire 4 takes the other 7 A out.
sol: Out: 3 + I.
I = 7 A, leaving the node.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 18 V with 3 Ω. Right branch: 12 V with 2 Ω. Shared resistor: 2 Ω. Find the voltage across the shared resistor.
questions.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 18 = 3I₁ + 2I₃; 12 = 2I₂ + 2I₃.
Solving: I₁ = 3 A, I₂ = 1.5 A, I₃ = 4.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 9 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 28 V with 2 Ω. Right branch: 15 V with 1 Ω. Shared resistor: 2 Ω. Find the current in the left battery.
questions.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 28 = 2I₁ + 2I₃; 15 = 1I₂ + 2I₃.
Solving: I₁ = 6.75 A, I₂ = 0.5 A, I₃ = 7.25 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 14.5 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 12 V with 1 Ω. Right branch: 12 V with 4 Ω. Shared resistor: 4 Ω. Find the current in the shared resistor.
questions.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 12 = 1I₁ + 4I₃; 12 = 4I₂ + 4I₃.
Solving: I₁ = 2 A, I₂ = 0.5 A, I₃ = 2.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 10 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 21 V with 4 Ω. Right branch: 16 V with 1 Ω. Shared resistor: 6 Ω. Find the power dissipated in the shared resistor.
questions.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 21 = 4I₁ + 6I₃; 16 = 1I₂ + 6I₃.
Solving: I₁ = 1.5 A, I₂ = 1 A, I₃ = 2.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 15 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 23 V with 2 Ω. Right branch: 20 V with 1 Ω. Shared resistor: 4 Ω. Find the current in the right battery.
questions.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 23 = 2I₁ + 4I₃; 20 = 1I₂ + 4I₃.
Solving: I₁ = 2.5 A, I₂ = 2 A, I₃ = 4.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 18 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries share a middle resistor. Left branch: 21 V with 4 Ω. Right branch: 27 V with 2 Ω. Shared resistor: 2 Ω. Find the current in the left battery.
questions.w: Use KCL at the top node and KVL on two loops (or a node voltage).
sol: I₃ = I₁ + I₂; 21 = 4I₁ + 2I₃; 27 = 2I₂ + 2I₃.
Solving: I₁ = 1.5 A, I₂ = 6 A, I₃ = 7.5 A.
Shared-resistor voltage = 15 V. Check: supplied power equals dissipated power.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A 12 V battery (1 Ω) and a 6 V battery (1 Ω) are in parallel (+ to +) across a 2 Ω load. Find the current in the 6 V battery, magnitude in amps. (It may be charging.)
questions.w: Find the common node voltage first, then each battery's current.
sol: Current out of the 6 V cell = (6 − 7.2)/1 = -1.2 A.
Negative means current flows INTO the 6 V battery: the stronger battery is charging it.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two voltage dividers sit across the same 12 V. Point P: 100 Ω above and 200 Ω below. Point Q: 300 Ω above and 100 Ω below. No wire joins P and Q. Find V_P − V_Q in volts.
questions.w: With no link, each divider is separate, so no loading.
sol: V_P − V_Q = 5 V. This is how a bridge detects an imbalance.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Three branches join at a top node and return to a common bottom node. Branch 1: 10 V source with 2 Ω. Branch 2: 4 V source with 1 Ω. Branch 3: just 4 Ω. Find the voltage across the 4 Ω resistor in volts.
questions.w: KCL at the top node: the two source branches deliver current, and the 4 Ω takes it.
sol: Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A circuit has 6 branches and 4 nodes. How many INDEPENDENT KVL loop equations are needed (using KCL at 3 of the nodes)?
questions.w: Independent loops = branches − nodes + 1.
sol: Independent KCL equations = nodes − 1 = 3.
Unknown currents = 6, so 6 equations are needed in all.
KVL loops needed = 6 − 3 = 3.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: In a network, the sources supply 40 W but the resistors dissipate 45 W. What should you conclude?
o: There is an error: power must balance
This is normal for parallel branches
questions.w: Energy is conserved, so supplied power equals dissipated power.
sol: Σ P(supplied) = Σ P(dissipated).
A mismatch means a mistake in signs or arithmetic.
Use the check to catch errors.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries: E₁ = 10 V (1 Ω) and E₂ = 4 V (2 Ω) are in parallel with a 2 Ω load. How much power does the 10 V source supply (E₁ × I₁)? Give watts.
questions.w: Find I₁ from the node voltage.
sol: Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Going from A to B along the top path you meet a 6 V rise then a 2 V drop. The bottom path has one element. By KVL, how many volts does the bottom element change the potential from A to B? (rise positive)
questions.w: The potential difference between two points is the same along every path.
sol: Top path: +6 − 2 = +4 V.
The bottom path must also give +4 V.
So the bottom element is a 4 V rise.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A loop has a 12 V battery and resistors R1 and R2 in series. A student writes 12 − IR1 + IR2 = 0. The error is:
o: IR2 should be a drop (−IR2), since the same current flows through it the same way
KVL should sum to the battery voltage, not zero
questions.w: Both resistors are drops going with the current: 12 − IR1 − IR2 = 0.
sol: Same current direction through both resistors.
Each makes a drop.
A sign flip on one resistor is the classic KVL mistake.
From your notes · Diodes and LEDs (area vii): Series LEDs: same current; drops add; the supply must exceed the sum.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Four wires meet at a junction: A brings in 3 A, B takes out 8 A, C brings in 2 A. Wire D carries current INTO the junction. How many amps?
questions.w: In = out: 3 + 2 + I_D = 8.
sol: Currents in: 3 + 2 + D.
Currents out: 8.
D = 3 A.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A 12 V battery (2 Ω) and a 3 V battery (1 Ω) are joined with OPPOSITE polarity across a shared 3 Ω resistor: the 3 V battery acts as −3 V at the top node. Find the voltage across the 3 Ω resistor in volts.
questions.w: Treat the reversed battery as a −3 V source and write one node equation.
sol: Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Two batteries E₁ = 12 V (R₁ = 2 Ω) and E₂ = 6 V (R₂ = 1 Ω) feed a shared 3 Ω resistor. Find the total power dissipated in all three resistors, in watts.
questions.w: Find the three currents, then add I²R, or use power supplied = E₁I₁ + E₂I₂.
sol: Supplied = 12 × 2.73 + 6 × -0.545 = 29.5 W, and I²R adds to 29.5 W.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A network has 5 nodes. How many independent KCL equations can you write?
questions.w: The last node's equation is just the sum of the others, so it adds nothing.
sol: Each node gives one KCL equation.
Add all five: every current appears once as in and once as out, giving 0 = 0.
So only 5 − 1 = 4 are independent.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: A single loop has a 9 V source, a 3 Ω resistor and an unknown resistor R. The 3 Ω has 6 V across it. What is R?
questions.w: KVL gives R's drop (3 V), and the loop current comes from the known resistor.
sol: Drop across R = 9 − 6 = 3 V.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Currents of 2.4 A and 0.9 A flow into a node, and 1.5 A flows out on a third wire. The fourth wire carries:
questions.w: Count everything in and everything out, then the leftover decides the direction.
sol: Out so far: 1.5 A.
Still 1.8 A must leave, so wire four carries 1.8 A out.
Notes|n7|Kirchhoff's laws (area ix, States and Nationals)

questions.q: Which 2-input gate is the exact opposite of OR (output flips for every input row)?
questions.w: NOR is OR followed by an inverter.
sol: OR is 1 for three rows and 0 only for (0,0).
Flip every output: 0 only for three rows, 1 only for (0,0).
That is NOR. NAND flips AND, not OR.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A binary number ends in 1. Is the number odd or even?
o: It depends on the other bits
Only odd if it has an even number of 1s
questions.w: The rightmost bit is worth 1; every other place value is even.
sol: Place values are 1, 2, 4, 8 ... Only the 1 is odd.
So the parity of the number is set by the last bit alone.
Misconception: counting 1s is parity of the bits, not of the number.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 2-input OR gate has one input held at 1. The output is:
o: the inverse of the other input
questions.w: OR with 1 gives 1 whatever the other input is.
sol: OR is 1 if at least one input is 1.
One input is already 1, so the output is locked at 1.
OR with 0 is the one that passes the other input.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: The 2-input gate outputs for inputs (A,B) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) are 1, 1, 1, 0. Which gate is it?
questions.w: NAND is 0 only when both inputs are 1.
sol: List where the output is 0: only (1,1).
AND gives 0 on three rows, so the opposite gate gives 0 on one row.
That is NAND.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: The 2-input gate outputs for (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1) are 1, 0, 0, 1. Which gate is it?
questions.w: Output is 1 when the inputs are equal.
sol: The 1s are at (0,0) and (1,1).
Both of those have equal inputs.
That is XNOR (equality). XOR would be 0, 1, 1, 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Even parity: a check bit is added so the total number of 1s is even. The data bits are 1011. What is the check bit?
questions.w: 1011 has three 1s, so a 1 makes four.
sol: Count the 1s in 1011: three.
Three is odd, so add a 1 to reach four (even).
The check bit equals the XOR of the data bits: 1⊕0⊕1⊕1 = 1.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: How many of the 16 rows of a 4-input AND gate output 0?
questions.w: AND is 1 only when all four inputs are 1.
sol: 2⁴ = 16 rows.
Only the row 1111 gives 1.
16 − 1 = 15 rows give 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: How many of the 16 rows of a 4-input XOR (1 when an odd number of inputs are 1) output 1?
questions.w: Odd parity is true for exactly half of the rows.
sol: Choose rows with one 1 (4 rows) or three 1s (4 rows).
Half of 16 is 8: flipping any one input flips the output.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 3-input XOR gives 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1. What is its output for A = 1, B = 1, C = 1?
questions.w: Three 1s is an odd count, so the output is 1.
sol: XOR in steps: 1⊕1 = 0.
Then 0⊕1 = 1.
Odd number of 1s gives 1.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Put the evaluation order for  A + B·C′  from FIRST to LAST.
questions.w: Precedence is NOT, then AND, then OR.
sol: NOT binds tightest.
AND comes before OR, like × before +.
OR is last.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For a 3-input gate, match each gate to how many of its 8 rows output 1.
questions.w: Count rows: AND needs all 1s; OR fails only at 000; XOR is odd parity.
sol: AND is 1 only at 111.
OR is 0 only at 000, so 7 rows are 1.
XOR is 1 when one or three inputs are 1: 3 + 1 = 4 rows.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = (A ⊕ B) + B·C equal to 1?
questions.w: Build the 8-row table in pieces and count the 1s.
sol: List all 8 (A,B,C) rows.
Work out each inner part first, then combine, following NOT before AND before OR.
Count the rows with output 1: 5.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = A′·(B ⊕ C) equal to 1?
questions.w: Build the 8-row table in pieces and count the 1s.
sol: List all 8 (A,B,C) rows.
Work out each inner part first, then combine, following NOT before AND before OR.
Count the rows with output 1: 2.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = NOR(AND(A,B), XOR(A,C)) equal to 1?
questions.w: Build the 8-row table in pieces and count the 1s.
sol: List all 8 (A,B,C) rows.
Work out each inner part first, then combine, following NOT before AND before OR.
Count the rows with output 1: 3.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = NOR( AND(A,B), XOR(A,C) ). Find Y for A = 1, B = 0, C = 1.
questions.w: AND = 0 and XOR = 0, so NOR(0,0) = 1.
sol: XOR(1,1) = 0 (equal inputs).
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = XOR( NAND(A,B), OR(B,C) ). Find Y for A = 1, B = 1, C = 0.
questions.w: NAND = 0, OR = 1, so XOR = 1.
sol: Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = AND( NOR(A,B), XNOR(B,C) ). For how many of the 8 input rows is Y = 1?
questions.w: NOR needs A = 0, B = 0; then XNOR needs C = 0.
sol: NOR(A,B) = 1 only when A = 0 and B = 0.
With B = 0, XNOR(B,C) = 1 only when C = 0.
Only the row 000 works: 1 row.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A′·B + A·B + A′·B′ simplifies to:
questions.w: A′B + AB = B, and B + A′B′ = A′ + B (using X + X′Y = X + Y).
sol: A′B + AB = B(A′ + A) = B.
Now B + A′B′ = B + A′ because B + B′Z = B + Z.
Result: A′ + B. Check A = 1, B = 0: every term is 0, so Y = 0, and A′ + B = 0 too.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: (A + B)·(A + B′) simplifies to:
questions.w: Expand: A + A·B′ + A·B + B·B′ = A + A(B′ + B) + 0 = A.
sol: Multiply out the brackets.
B·B′ = 0 and A·B + A·B′ = A.
So A + A = A. Spot check: A = 0 makes both brackets B and B′, and B·B′ = 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A·B + A′·C + B·C simplifies to:
questions.w: The B·C term is redundant (consensus): when B·C = 1, either A·B or A′·C is already 1.
sol: Look at B·C = 1. Then B = 1 and C = 1.
If A = 1, A·B = 1. If A = 0, A′·C = 1.
So B·C never adds a new 1 and can be removed.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: (A ⊕ B) ⊕ B simplifies to:
questions.w: XOR with B twice cancels: B ⊕ B = 0 and A ⊕ 0 = A.
sol: XOR is associative: A ⊕ (B ⊕ B).
B ⊕ B = 0 (equal inputs).
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: XNOR(A,B) = (A ⊕ B)′ is also equal to:
questions.w: Inverting one XOR input inverts the output.
sol: XOR with 1 inverts the other input.
Inverting one input flips the result: (A ⊕ B′) = (A ⊕ B)′.
Inverting both inputs cancels: A′ ⊕ B′ = A ⊕ B, the opposite.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: By De Morgan, (A·B·C)′ equals:
questions.w: Break the bar, flip the operator, complement each variable.
sol: Break the long bar over the AND.
AND becomes OR.
Each variable gets its own bar.
From your notes · Digital logic and binary (area viii): Break the bar, flip the operator.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: By De Morgan, (A + B′ + C)′ equals:
questions.w: OR becomes AND and every term is complemented, including B′ becoming B.
sol: Break the bar, change + to ·.
Complement each term: A′, (B′)′ = B, C′.
Do not forget B′ flips to B (double negation).
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build a NOR gate?
questions.w: NOR = NOT(OR); OR takes 3 NAND gates and the final inverter is a 4th.
sol: OR from NANDs: 2 inverters + 1 NAND = 3 gates.
NOR is OR inverted.
One more NAND wired as an inverter: 3 + 1 = 4.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the minimum number of 2-input NAND gates needed to build an AND gate?
questions.w: NAND then an inverter (a NAND with tied inputs).
sol: AND = NOT(NAND).
NAND is 1 gate.
Inverter is a second NAND: 2 gates.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the minimum number of 2-input NOR gates needed to build an XNOR gate? (Use the circuit N = NOR(A,B), then NOR(A,N) and NOR(B,N), then NOR of those two.)
questions.w: The four-gate NOR design gives XNOR.
sol: N = A′B′.
NOR(A,N) = A′B and NOR(B,N) = AB′.
NOR of those = (A′B + AB′)′ = XNOR. Four gates.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A circuit is NAND( NAND(A,A), NAND(B,B) ). It behaves as which single gate?
questions.w: The inner NANDs are inverters, so the output is (A′·B′)′ = A + B.
sol: NAND(A,A) = A′ and NAND(B,B) = B′.
Outer: (A′·B′)′.
De Morgan: = A + B, an OR gate.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = NAND( A, NAND(A,B) ). Which expression equals Y?
questions.w: NAND(A,B) = A′ + B′. Then Y = (A·(A′ + B′))′ = (A·B′)′ = A′ + B.
sol: Inner NAND = (AB)′ = A′ + B′.
Y = (A·B′)′ = A′ + B. It is 0 only for A = 1, B = 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 3-input function has Y = 1 for ABC = 001, 011, 101, 111 and Y = 0 otherwise. Y equals:
questions.w: Every 1 row has C = 1, and every row with C = 1 is a 1 row.
sol: Look at the column C in the four 1 rows: always 1.
A and B take all four combinations.
So Y ignores A and B: Y = C.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 3-input function has Y = 1 for ABC = 000, 001, 110, 111 and 0 otherwise. Y equals:
o: A·B + A′·B′ (XNOR of A and B)
questions.w: C does not matter. Y = 1 exactly when A = B.
sol: The 1 rows pair up: 000 and 001 differ only in C.
Same for 110 and 111, so C drops out.
Left: A = B = 0 or A = B = 1, which is XNOR.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = 1 for ABC = 011, 101, 110, 111 (at least two inputs are 1). Which expression matches?
questions.w: Each pair of 1s makes Y = 1: AB, AC or BC.
sol: The rows with two or more 1s each contain a pair (AB, AC or BC).
OR the three pair terms.
A ⊕ B ⊕ C is wrong because it is 0 for 011.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 4:1 mux has S1 = A, S0 = B and data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 = 0, 1, 1, 0. The output is:
questions.w: Output is 1 only for AB = 01 and 10: XOR.
sol: S1S0 = AB picks the input numbered AB in binary.
I1 (AB = 01) and I2 (AB = 10) are 1.
1 when A and B differ: XOR.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 2:1 mux has select = A, I0 = 1 and I1 = B. The output is:
questions.w: A = 0 gives 1; A = 1 passes B.
sol: Select 0 picks I0 = 1.
Select 1 picks I1 = B.
Y = 1 unless A = 1 and B = 0, which is A′ + B.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: To build any 3-input function with an 8:1 mux, connect A, B, C to the select lines. What goes on the 8 data inputs?
o: The 8 output values of the truth table (0 or 1 each)
The inputs A, B and C repeated
Only the rows where the output is 1, one per input
questions.w: Each select combination picks one data input, so that input just holds the output for that row.
sol: 8 select combinations = 8 rows.
Row k is picked by select value k.
Tie input k to 1 or 0 to match the table.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: For how many of the 8 input rows is the Carry-out of a full adder equal to 1?
questions.w: Carry is 1 when at least two of the three inputs are 1.
sol: Carry means the sum is 2 or 3.
Rows with two 1s: 3. Rows with three 1s: 1.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: How many full adders does an 8-bit ripple-carry adder with a carry input use?
questions.w: One full adder per bit position.
sol: Each bit adds A, B and the carry from the right.
That is a full adder.
8 bits means 8 full adders.
From your notes · Digital logic and binary (area viii): A ripple adder chains full adders.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: In a ripple-carry adder, why does the top sum bit settle later than the bottom one?
o: The carry must pass through each stage in turn
The top bits are larger numbers
The sum bits use a different clock
questions.w: Each stage waits for the carry from the stage to its right.
sol: Stage 0 makes carry c1.
Stage 1 needs c1 before it can make c2, and so on.
The delay adds up along the chain.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the largest number that fits in 8 binary bits? Give the answer in decimal.
sol: 8 bits give 2⁸ = 256 patterns.
They start at 0.
So the largest is 255.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Adding a 0 on the right end of a binary number (for example 101 becomes 1010) does what to its value?
questions.w: Every bit moves one place to the left, so every place value doubles.
sol: Each bit now sits in a place worth twice as much.
Same idea as adding a 0 in decimal multiplies by 10.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Subtract in binary: 10010 − 1011. Give the answer in binary.
sol: Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: A 4-bit adder adds 1111 + 1111. What 5-bit result comes out?
sol: Each number is 15.
So 11110: carry-out 1 and sum bits 1110.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: Y = A·B + A·C′. A student wants fewer gates. Which factored form equals Y?
questions.w: Factor out A: A·B + A·C′ = A·(B + C′).
sol: Both terms share A.
Distributive law reverses.
Check A = 0: Y = 0 and A(B + C′) = 0. (A + B)(A + C′) would be wrong because it is 1 when B = C′ = 1 and A = 0.
Notes|n10|Digital logic and binary (area viii)

questions.q: What is the contrapositive of P → Q?
questions.w: The contrapositive swaps and negates both parts, and it always has the same truth value as the original.
sol: Converse: Q → P (swap only).
Inverse: ~P → ~Q (negate only).
Contrapositive: swap AND negate = ~Q → ~P.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Statement: "If the switch is closed, the lamp lights." What is its converse?
o: If the lamp lights, the switch is closed.
If the switch is open, the lamp is off.
If the lamp is off, the switch is open.
The switch is closed and the lamp lights.
questions.w: The converse swaps the if-part and the then-part.
sol: Original: if S then L.
Swap the two parts only: if L then S.
The converse is NOT equivalent to the original: a lamp can light for other reasons.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Statement: "If the switch is closed, the lamp lights." What is its inverse?
o: If the switch is open, the lamp does not light.
If the lamp lights, the switch is closed.
If the lamp is off, the switch is open.
The switch is open or the lamp lights.
questions.w: The inverse negates both parts but keeps the order.
sol: Original: if S then L.
Negate both parts, keep the order: if not S then not L.
The inverse is NOT equivalent to the original, but it is the contrapositive of the converse.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Switch logic: switches in series = AND (both closed to light).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which statement is logically equivalent to P → Q?
questions.w: P → Q fails only when P is true and Q is false, and ~P ∨ Q fails in exactly that row.
sol: P → Q is false only for P = T, Q = F.
~P ∨ Q is false only when ~P is F and Q is F, i.e. P = T, Q = F.
The tables match.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which statement is the negation of P → Q?
questions.w: The only way an if-then fails is when the if-part is true and the then-part is false.
sol: Ask when P → Q is false: P true, Q false.
Write that as P ∧ ~Q.
Misconception: the negation of an if-then is NOT another if-then.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: By De Morgan and double negation, ~(P ∧ ~Q) is equivalent to:
questions.w: Flip ∧ to ∨ and negate each part: ~P ∨ ~~Q = ~P ∨ Q.
sol: Break the bar over the AND.
Negate P and negate ~Q.
~~Q = Q, so ~P ∨ Q (which is P → Q).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which pair of statements are logically equivalent to each other?
o: The converse and the inverse of the same if-then
questions.w: Converse is Q → P; inverse is ~P → ~Q. These are contrapositives of each other.
sol: Take the contrapositive of Q → P: ~P → ~Q.
That is exactly the inverse.
So they always match each other, but not the original.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: In how many of the 4 rows of a truth table is (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P) true?
questions.w: That is P ↔ Q: true when P and Q match.
sol: Rows (T,T) and (F,F) have P = Q.
Rows (T,F) and (F,T) break one direction.
2 rows.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: In how many of the 8 rows of a truth table for P, Q, R is (P → Q) → R true?
questions.w: Work out P → Q first, then the outer if-then.
sol: R true: always makes the outer if-then true (4 rows).
R false: need (P → Q) false, i.e. P = T, Q = F (1 row).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: In how many of the 8 rows is P → (Q → R) true?
questions.w: It is false only when P is T, Q is T and R is F.
sol: The outer if-then fails only if P is T and Q → R is F.
Q → R is F only for Q = T, R = F.
1 failing row, so 8 − 1 = 7.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: A statement that is true in every row of its truth table, like P ∨ ~P, is called a ______.
questions.w: A tautology is always true.
sol: Check P true: P ∨ ~P is true.
Check P false: ~P is true, so still true.
Always true means tautology.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Given P → Q is true and Q is true. What can you conclude about P?
o: Nothing; P may be true or false
questions.w: A true Q is consistent with P true or false: affirming the consequent is invalid.
sol: With Q true, P → Q is true whatever P is.
So P can be T or F.
No conclusion follows.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Premises: P → Q and ~P. Which conclusion follows validly?
o: None of the usual conclusions (~Q is not forced)
questions.w: Denying the antecedent proves nothing about Q.
sol: Try P = F, Q = T: both premises true.
Then ~Q is false, so ~Q is not forced.
Q is also not forced (Q = F works).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Which is the correct translation of "The relay clicks only if the switch is closed"? (R = relay clicks, S = switch closed)
questions.w: "Only if" points to the necessary condition: the click needs the closed switch.
sol: If the relay clicks, the switch must have been closed.
So R is the "if" part: R → S.
Misconception: "only if" does not mean S → R.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Translate: "The lamp is lit if the switch is closed." (L = lamp lit, S = switch closed)
questions.w: A plain "if" introduces the condition: closed switch is sufficient for a lit lamp.
sol: "X if Y" means Y → X.
Y is the closed switch.
So S → L.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Translate "P and Q are not both true."
questions.w: "Not both" negates the whole AND.
sol: Put the bar over the entire P ∧ Q.
Neither P nor Q would be ~P ∧ ~Q (both false), which is stronger.
~(P ∧ Q) = ~P ∨ ~Q by De Morgan.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let D = battery is dead, S = switch is open, L = lamp is off. "If the battery is dead or the switch is open, then the lamp is off."
questions.w: The "if" part contains the OR group.
sol: The comma after "open" marks the end of the if-part.
The if-part is D ∨ S.
So (D ∨ S) → L.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let D = battery is dead, S = switch is open, L = lamp is off. "The lamp is off only if the battery is dead or the switch is open."
questions.w: "Only if" puts the lamp-off on the if side.
sol: Lamp off needs a cause: D or S.
So L implies D ∨ S.
(D ∨ S) → L is the converse.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Let L = lamp is on, S = switch is closed, B = battery is charged. "The lamp is on if and only if the switch is closed and the battery is charged."
questions.w: "If and only if" is ↔; the group S ∧ B sits on the right.
sol: "If and only if" is the double arrow.
Both conditions (S and B) are grouped.
So L ↔ (S ∧ B).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Switch A is in series with a parallel pair of switches B and C. The lamp is on when:
questions.w: The parallel pair works like OR, and the series link with A works like AND.
sol: B and C in parallel: B ∨ C.
That block is in series with A: AND.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Switches A and B in series form one branch. A switch C forms a second branch in parallel with it. The lamp is on when:
questions.w: Each branch is a way for current to flow: either A and B both closed, or C closed.
sol: Branch 1 works if A ∧ B.
Branch 2 works if C.
Parallel branches: OR of the two.
From your notes · Control devices (area vi): Switch logic: switches in series = AND (both closed to light).
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Proof lines: 1. A → B (P)  2. B → C (P)  3. A (P)  4. B (MP 1,3)  5. C (?). The reason for line 5 is:
questions.w: Line 5 uses B → C and B, which is modus ponens.
sol: Need an if-then and its antecedent.
Line 2 is B → C and line 4 gives B.
That is MP. HS would give A → C, not C.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Proof lines: 1. P ∨ Q (P)  2. ~P (P)  3. Q (DS 1,2)  4. Q → R (P)  5. R (?). The reason for line 5 is:
questions.w: Q is true (line 3) and Q → R, so R by modus ponens.
sol: Look for an if-then with a true antecedent.
Line 4 is Q → R and line 3 is Q.
That is MP.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Proof lines: 1. ~A ∨ B (P)  2. A (P)  3. ~~A (DN 2)  4. B (?). The reason for line 4 is:
questions.w: Disjunctive syllogism needs the NEGATION of one side of the OR. The negation of ~A is ~~A (line 3).
sol: Line 1 is ~A ∨ B.
To use DS we must deny ~A, which means having ~~A.
Line 3 does that, so B follows by DS from 1 and 3.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: ~(P ∧ Q), P ∴ ~Q. Is this argument valid?
o: Valid only if Q is false already
questions.w: ~(P ∧ Q) is ~P ∨ ~Q by De Morgan; with P true, ~P is false, so ~Q.
sol: De Morgan: ~P ∨ ~Q.
P is true, so ~P is false.
Disjunctive syllogism leaves ~Q.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: P → Q and ~P → R. Does Q ∨ R follow?
o: Yes; either P or ~P is true, so Q or R
No; the premises share no letter
Only if Q and R are both true
questions.w: Constructive dilemma with P ∨ ~P (a tautology) as the third premise.
sol: P ∨ ~P is always true.
If P, then Q. If ~P, then R.
So Q ∨ R in every case.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: Premises: P → (Q → R), P, Q. Which conclusion follows?
questions.w: MP on P gives Q → R; MP again with Q gives R.
sol: P → (Q → R) and P give Q → R (MP).
Q → R and Q give R (MP).
Two modus ponens steps.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: P → Q, R → Q, Q ∴ P ∨ R. Is this valid?
questions.w: Q can be true for a third reason, with P and R both false.
sol: Constructive dilemma needs P ∨ R as a premise, not Q.
Try P = F, R = F, Q = T.
All premises true, conclusion false.
Notes|n11|Symbolic logic (optional, but quick points)

questions.q: P → Q and P → R. Which conclusion follows?
questions.w: If P is true, both Q and R must be true.
sol: Assume P.
Then Q by the first premise and R by the second.
So P → (Q ∧ R). The converse does not follow.

sol: Substitute the values.
Work out each smaller piece.
Combine to get 1.

questions.q: Let A = 1, B = 0, C = 0 (1 = true, 0 = false). Find the value of (A ∨ B) → (A ∧ B). Give 1 or 0.

sol: Substitute the values.
Work out each smaller piece.
Combine to get 0.

questions.q: Let A = 0, B = 1, C = 1 (1 = true, 0 = false). Find the value of ~(A → B) ∨ ~C. Give 1 or 0.

sol: Substitute the values.
Work out each smaller piece.
Combine to get 0.
